The other thing I think about when I think about giving myself permission to look away is that suffering and serving are hard to do at the same time. You have to step out of your suffering to help serve others. And sometimes you serving your people is the best way to help and to contribute to the world.

I have very few people who I know who are actual, like their coaching niches and what they do actually does serve people during tragic times. Like I have the friend of mine who married us, she is a coach for first responders and firefighters. And so she actually goes to fire zones to coach and help the mental health of the people responding and dealing days on end with no sleep and death. And so that’s amazing and it’s perfect.

But your best service may be, your best service to humanity could be you helping your people all the time, no matter what. It could also be jumping in to help things that are happening and to serve in other ways, but just know suffering and serving are hard to do at the same time. It’s just impossible to serve others when you’re lost in your own suffering. So I’m always thinking about the ways to keep myself serving and helping and contributing. And so I just know I can’t be like really living in the suffering all the time. It’s not good.

Which brings me to my next point. You’ve heard me say this if you’ve listened to the podcast for any amount of time or been in my programs, but I consider myself the asset. And I talk about that a lot and what it means. And in this instance, I am the asset to more than myself. This isn’t selfish, right? This is recognizing that other people use me as an asset and rely on me as an asset. And that’s important to know. It’s a big job when someone’s relying on you as their asset for their life and their business, and their success. So even more than I’m the asset to my own family and to my own company, I am the asset to my audience and my clients.

We are coaches. I want you to think about this. We don’t believe, most of us do not believe, that taking care of oneself is selfish. So then why would we think that taking care of our business during a tragedy is tone deaf? Which is what the question in my 2k for 2k community was about. She was saying, you know, I’m really struggling to post for my business right now. She’s like, it just feels so heavy and so hard with what’s happening in the world that, you know, in this specific instance, while in real time, there was just a massive, unimaginable flash flood in Texas that took the lives of many people, including many young children, young girls. And it’s been hard for a lot of people, including myself. And so she was feeling like it just feels impossible to post, wrong to post. And if she posted anything, it would just feel tone deaf.

But businesses have people to help. They have customers to respond to, they have employees to pay, they have products to deliver. They have people waiting for them to show up. And so I don’t think it’s tone deaf for business to continue happening. Like the banker has to go to work because someone needs a withdrawal today. Even if they’re, what I call carrying the heavy purse, they have heavy emotions with them, they still have to go to work. And businesses are the same. In fact, small businesses are the hardest because there’s very few people. There’s not, it’s not like if you call in sick, somebody else can fill in. There’s no one else to fill in for the CEO’s job, for the coach’s job.

So this week in particular, in this instance, in this tragedy, in this moment of time, I had 100, over 100 students waiting. Some of them up to six years. Like today, I, this is Mastermind Week for 200k. And today, I, it was day two on marketing and I asked them as part of the lesson, how long they’d, from the time they heard about 200k to the time they signed up, how long it took. And so many of them, there were a couple of people that said a month, you know, six months, but many of them said one year, two years, three years, four years, five years, six years. Like so many people said between three and six years. They have been waiting that long to participate in Mastermind Week.

So I had to be filled up, not depleted, no matter how tragic and sad world events are. And in this case, I was on vacation when I heard about the Texas floods, and I, again, I could not stop thinking about the parents, thinking about the girls, thinking about reading all the different stories, like telling my husband about the stories. Like I was truly gutted and still am. And I have 100 people waiting six years to participate in Mastermind Week. So I have to be filled up. I can’t be lost in the sadness.

I think in the beginning and in the earlier stages of business, I think it is easier for you to get swallowed up in the grief and seeing everything on social and feeling weird to post or to market or to show up at all for your business, but only because you aren’t believing people are waiting for you. Because when you have people waiting for you and relying on you, when you are their asset, as a leader, you have to move forward. As a business, you have to move forward.

And I was thinking about this because this year, especially, with so many things that have happened in the world that have really caused me to grieve, I’ve also had so many things on my schedule. So many ways to help people. That there has not been, because I’m having a baby and going on maternity leave, there was not one week that could be pushed back. I worked sick three, four, five times this year. Like, sometimes really sick. Like with norovirus, with a chronic sinus infection. Like I have worked very sick this year because there’s just no time. There wasn’t an availability to push something back.

And let’s say I just canceled something. Okay, so let’s imagine if something terrible and tragic had happened when I was scheduled to sell Capacity Work, for example. And there’s no time to reschedule, so I just cancel. Then the 600 people who did Capacity Work, who said it was my best work yet, and to this day, it is still changing their life, would have missed out on that. If I decided it would be tone deaf to sell during a tragic time. But I just can’t. There’s no room to push it back. So I’ve got to do it.

If something happens during a launch schedule, I got to do it. I don’t think that’s tone deaf. I think that’s a mature business. That’s knowing and being very aware and conscious that people are waiting for you. They’ve been waiting for you. They invested a lot of money with you. They’re thinking of investing a lot of money with you. That you are their asset. It’s understanding leadership.

So I just don’t lose, the state of where I’m at in my business, I don’t lose work days anymore to grieving things that didn’t happen to me. I want you to hear that. I know it’s hard to hear, but I do not lose work days anymore to grieving things that did not happen personally to me. If it did happen personally to me, not in my community, like we had a mass shooting in my community this year. I had to work that day.

In fact, I had a live event at my in my city that I think the same week, it was terrifying. I ended up hiring security because I was so terrified. I just wanted all my people to be safe. I wanted to be safe. We spent like $1200 having armed security guards because I just was so shook. And I had to record my three-year plan live in front of an audience. Like that was scheduled, people were flying in, that was already happening. That is a mature business.

So I don’t lose the work days to grieving things that didn’t happen to me. If something does happen to me, I took a week off when my dog died. If it happened to me, I will grieve those things. But if it’s something that happened in the world that caught that I feel grief for and empathy for, I do that in my personal time. I do that on the weekends. I do that on the in the mornings. I do that at lunch. I do that in the evening. I give myself time to think about it and to process it.

I have written letters that I wouldn’t send, but I’ve written letters to people that I don’t know that have been through tragic things that I’m just feeling so sad for them and I just want to say all the things to them and that’s been really healing for me to just, like if I could send them a letter, if I could give them a message, this is what I would say. Like I’ve done that work, like very intentional grieving if you have listened to my podcast about how I grieved my dog. Like I grieve, I feel like I grieve very intentionally.

But I do it in my personal time if it didn’t happen directly to me, because I do have employees and I do have clients depending on me. I am their asset.

The other thing I was thinking about is like today especially, I have a toddler depending on me too. All smiles, ready to play, needing mommy to be mommy, not mommy crying all day scrolling the news feed. And not all of you may have young children or children who rely on you, but that is something to think about. It’s like our families need us and they don’t need us to be scrolling the news feed, crying all day.

The other thing I want you to think about that I mentioned earlier, but I think is worth its own space on this episode, is remember the way the algorithm works. It shows you a terrible thing, you engage, and then it shows you more terrible things until all you see is news from the terrible thing. That is the way it works. That’s the way the news works. We’re going to show you, we’re going to talk about all these terrible things, scare the crap out of you, make you feel awful, keep highlighting the tragic events so that you keep watching, so that we keep getting our ad spend, so that we keep getting paid from YouTube or paid from Instagram, right?

Accounts are actively creating like click-worthy content to keep you on the platform, consuming. But is that the best thing for you and your business and your clients and your audience? Is it the healthiest thing? Now, again, spend time purposely if you want to hear the stories, and you want to read up on it, and you want to grieve alongside humanity. That’s the way I think about it, and I do that.

But truly, I recommend giving yourself a time limit to come back to your world and your life. And then use that empathy to donate time, money, resources, if that feels good, versus just endlessly consuming the news and the terrible things that are coming out and all the stories. Give yourself some time in your own time, but don’t get lost in I can’t work because I’m so distraught if it didn’t personally happen to you.

And then, I want you to think about this. This one’s probably the hardest, but what would your energy and your business be like if you didn’t let the news into your world for just six months? Even 30 days. We really think that we have to be looking, we have to be up to date, we have to know all the terrible things. We have to make sure that we’re not tone deaf.

But one of the greatest things I ever did for my business is master coach training, and the one of the first things they said in master coach training is over the next six months, we’re going to transform your entire life, everything about you. You have the opportunity to really develop coaching mastery. But you’re going to need all of your energy and all of your brain space, and you’re really going to have to focus on you and your self-improvement and like really owning your life. And there’s not going to be room for focusing on everything else.

So they asked us to take a break from the news and not watch or consume any news, whether it was on the actual TV or on the news feed, but to not consume any news for the entire program, which was six months. And I listened to that. And I changed my life so dramatically. I saw the difference of all of the places my energy was being sucked dry.

I lost 30 pounds. I completely transformed my 2k for 2k program. I created 200k Mastermind and sold it, and created $300,000 in a couple of months period. I changed myself as a leader. I got better at my coaching. I worked on some deep relationships with family members. Like, I literally changed everything about myself because I had the energy to do it, because I was focused 100% on me. And that could seem selfish, but now you have the version of me recording these podcasts and creating the entrepreneur series and coaching in 2k and 200k and a 2 Million Dollar Group. Like you get the version of me now because I was willing to be the asset back then.

And so I want you to think about treating yourself that way. Treating yourself like there is inside of you a capacity, a brilliance, a thought leader, a true transformative coach that is going to deeply impact the world. And every second you lose yourself in the things happening in the world, you lose your energy to do that quickly and then help the people who you’re meant to help. And so you have to look at the tradeoff.

I can grieve this endlessly and miss days of work and not post and not market and not sell and not do my business and take breaks every time something terrible happens. And I say that knowing the weight of all the things I’ve grieved this year and also knowing that over 10 years, there’s been an insurmountable amount of things that have happened. Like innumerable, that’s the word I meant. Innumerable amount of things that have happened.

It would take me too long to list all of the terrible things that have happened in the last 10 years. And if I stopped running my business every time they happened, you would not have me on this podcast today right now giving you this message or any of the other messages I’ve given you. You wouldn’t have the leader that I am today. And you wouldn’t have my experience, having sold forty million dollars of coaching. You wouldn’t have the data study and the proven processes that I’ve created. You wouldn’t have any of that.

So think about really, truly what’s on the table for you if you can just focus on you and that feels right and really own you becoming your sharpest version of you to impact the world.

Okay, so here are my final thoughts. If you are grieving and you are feeling deep empathy and you need to take time, take it. I also want to say that. I don’t think anything is going to happen to your business dramatically if you’re offline for a few days. Like in the scheme of things, if you take two days to be offline, even if you’re working and you’re coaching clients, but you’re just not posting doesn’t feel right, nothing’s going to happen for a few days. But just be careful how often you let that happen.

And then a question that we get a lot is your content can reflect what’s happening in the world. You can do that. You could offer support to people who might be grieving or having a hard time with what they’re going through or what they’re seeing. But I will tell you, more often than not, when the news feed is slammed with coverage, I actually think people appreciate seeing something else. Because there’s just only so much you can take. And you could be the breath of fresh air. That is an option. Right? Like there were times where I’m like, okay, I’ve consumed enough. I have to like unfollow everyone presenting me with this because it’s just, I got to lead. I’ve got people relying on me.

Like this week, I’m not only doing 200k masterminds mastermind week, but most of my core program calls, and I’m recording my launch audit course, and I’m recording podcasts, and I have a baby at home or a toddler at home. I still refer to him as my baby. I have got a lot going on. There’s a time where I’m like, okay, I have to just, you know, I’m going to take a couple days and then I’m closing social media and I’m getting back to business. And I’ve got to just focus. I got to be the asset this week.

So I don’t think anything’s dramatic is going to happen if you take a few days from posting off or you post about what’s happening for a few days. Just be careful about how long you let that happen. And then you don’t have to pause your post, or you don’t have to, your post don’t have to reflect everything that’s always happening in the world. You get to be the breath of fresh air.

Now, if you feel your people are directly impacted or your community is, then lead and keep leading. But don’t get swallowed whole. Don’t forget what your people most want. Don’t forget the infinite game. The infinite game requires more commitment to what you infinitely want long-term to create than the finite present time.

There’s a great book on this by Simon, is it Simon Sinek? Simon Sinek. I don’t know how to pronounce his last name. But it’s called The Infinite Game and it’s so good and has really changed my perspective to keep me focused on my mission and what I’m creating, no matter what’s happening present in present time. And so I think about that often.

And then this is also the time to emotionally regulate and increase your capacity to hold duality. To hold running a business and feeling so deeply for people going through the unimaginable. You are actually capable of doing both. You can hold both of those things.

But the final thing I think I’ll share with you is that during these times when I feel really awkward, like that does come up for me too. Like, oh, should I not post? Like, what should I post? Should I say something? Should I not say something? I always imagine the people who have to get up and go to work. Even in the areas affected, the bankers, the hospital workers, the grocery store clerks, those people don’t have the privilege, and I’m saying that, privilege to sit at home all day online thinking they are too upset to work. That’s maybe the hardest thing that I’m going to say on this episode, but it is true.

We do this with entrepreneurship when we’re not seeing our business the same as an actual job, and when we have the privilege to just not work, to take a day off. Most of the world does not have that privilege. We would not call a nurse tone deaf for showing up to the hospital. We wouldn’t call the banker tone deaf. You know, anyone that shows, gets up, and goes to work, we wouldn’t call them tone deaf. We wouldn’t think of them that way. So why do we think of ourselves that way? Got to show up, we got to go to work. Even when it’s hard.

That’s when we hold it. We hold leadership. We hold what our people most want. We regulate ourselves, and we hold the terrible things that are also happening and the deep tragedies that other people are experiencing. Maybe we even hold gratitude, deep gratitude.

Like I remember feeling like when the news first broke of the flooding, I was at the Four Seasons, Walt Disney World in Orlando. And I remember telling my husband, it feels so crazy to me that we are at this beautiful five-star resort. My son is running through the splash pad, having so much fun. We’re being catered food, you know, going to Disney World. Like we’re doing the most luxurious things, and someone’s baby is being washed away in the river. Like it just sometimes blows my mind. It really does. Like it’s like it truly is unimaginable. I really do get it. It feels wild.

And so I was telling him like, the remaining trip, it was like every second I felt so grateful. And I felt that way this entire time. I took my son, I worked all day today, and then it’s been really hot here in Louisville, so I took my son to the pool after I finished working. I’m back working now. I’m recording this episode. But we took a little break, a couple hour break, and I took him to the pool, and I just, it was in the back of my head. Like what a luxury, what a privilege. I’m so grateful that I get to be splashing in the pool with my child right now. Like what a time.

And so I do think that we can hold gratitude as well, deep gratitude. At the same time as deep empathy. I think we can hold them both. I think we’re capable. We have the capacity inside of us. If anybody does, it’s us coaches. But don’t let the empathy and the grief swallow you.

I know it’s a hard, it’s a hard message to say, but I’ve got to say it to all of you. Because you’re going to hear a lot in your entire lifetime of your business, there’s going to be a lot that happens. There’s going to be a lot that fills the news feed. And you’ve got to just decide. And maybe it’s each time, right? Because some things will feel closer to home than others.

But I’ve seen people with really big businesses not be able to move past something happening in the world and lose tons of money in their business because they just can’t, they let the thing happening take over their entire world, their entire conversations, and they stop thinking about their infinite game and their movement and the impact they’re having and they step out of that.

And my job as your business coach is always going to be to fight for your mission and your purpose and your people and the work that you’re doing in the world. So this is my viewpoint. You don’t have to agree with it. You don’t have to take it on. You can take on the pieces that feel useful and helpful.

But you know, I was thinking about, I recorded episodes when COVID-19 first hit and the world shut down, and I was thinking like, those just don’t feel like they are right for some of the things that have happened this year in the world, specifically, that I’ve grieved. And so I wanted to have this episode that felt a little more mature and a little more connected. And so I really do hope this is helpful, but that’s the only desire I have is for this to be helpful and for it not in any way to be anything other than that.

So take what’s helpful, take what’s useful. You know, if you’re one of my clients, I’m happy to dive into the discussion even more, help you through the nuance. Of course, there is always nuance, but I do think this is a good episode to save and a good place to start every time people ask these questions in my communities. I think this would be a great way for me to say this is my official answer for most situations.

Okay. I know this was a heavy one. I know it was a hard one. I do love you all. If, you know, it landed, I’m so happy. If not, you can come back to it when you’re ready. Sometimes we’re just ready to hear things in one moment than another. And next week we’ll be get back to our regularly scheduled content. All right. I’ll see you next week. Bye-bye.

Hey, if you’re ready to make money as a life coach, I want to invite you to join my 2K for 2K program; where you’re going to make your first $2,000 the hardest part using my simple five-step formula for getting consults and closing new clients. Just head over to StaceyBoehman.com/2Kfor2K. We’ll see you inside.

title: Ep #344: Business Debt
transcript:
Welcome
 to the 
Make Money as a Life Coach
®
 
podcast
 
where sales expert and Master Coach Stacey Boehman teaches you how to make your first $2K, $20K, and $200K using her proven formula.

Hi coaches, welcome to episode 344. Today we’re going to talk about business debt and all the different types of debt that can come with a business.

The reason why I wanted to have this episode is as I, I just finished my Entrepreneur Series, ROI. We did a lot of coaching on a lot of things. And one of the things that came up was investment debt and what I found is there are coaches, a lot of coaches, who have either an aversion to any sort of business debt or a lot of shame about having any sort of debt, whether it’s credit card debt or actual line of credit and not having really positive thoughts or useful thoughts to either get the debt paid down, not get in the debt, or in any way manage the debt.

And so I wanted to do an episode about this because I think I have some really positive thoughts about it, not like, oh, debt is great, but I just think my thoughts are very useful. And I also think I have a more wide perspective when it comes to entrepreneurship that I think could be helpful too. So, you want to dive in? Let’s do it.

There’s a couple of distinctions when it comes to debt that I want to make. So the first one is, there is a difference between investment debt and business debt. And that is really important when you are contemplating debt or are trying to manage debt. It’s really important that you, just in general for financial literacy and for financial confidence and believing you are financially responsible, I think the more neutral that you can be, I think the more aware you can be, and educated you can be, I think the better it goes.

So, investment debt is not quite the same as business debt. There are different things. And you could have both at the same time. But business debt comes from things like paying yourself, employees, software expenses, marketing expenses. Basically, what I would consider for coaches, I’m just talking about coaches, anything non-coaching related. So anything that you are not… masterminds, one-on-one coaching, programs, anything you would buy to get coached or to learn something, any type of investment you would make into your brain or your skill set.

Business debt is everything that’s not that. So, for example, let’s say you’re making $100,000, but you have $140,000 of expenses, and those expenses are because you have software expenses and marketing expenses, and employees, and you’re also paying yourself. Like all of those things factor into more money going out than is coming in, and then a requirement to take on debt to pay those bills. So that’s what I would consider business debt.

Then investment debt is coaching, programs, certifications, mentorships, things like that. Now, we’re going to talk about this in a second, but where it gets really tricky is when you have both of those things happening at the same time. What I’ve noticed is that coaches don’t typically give credit to overspending in expenses, and they will blame all of the debt on the coaching programs and certifications and mentorships.

But if I start talking to them about it, turns out they’re paying themselves, they’re paying a VA, they have some, you know, random software expenses, they have other things they’re spending their money on in their business that aren’t just the investment. So then it becomes a little bit tricky. We’ll talk about that in a second.

But then, when you think about debt, I think it’s also important to talk about consumer debt. Consumer debt is buying things for personal use. And in this conversation, I want to point out that buying a house, I consider consumer debt.

A lot of people consider buying a house investment debt, like this is an investment. But unless you’re actually investing in real estate to sell for a profit, if you are just buying a home to live in, then it’s not really an investment because or unless you pay cash for it, and or you can pay it off so quickly that it can then appreciate and then you sell and you get the profit of it. But if you’re going to live in this house and you’re going to pay on it for thirty years, typically what you will find is you will pay double for the house than you actually bought, and it would require you living in the house probably way beyond thirty years for it to finally appreciate more than the double that you paid for, right?

So if you paid a million dollars for a house and then you actually, you finance it, so it ends up costing two million over thirty years, then that house has to then be worth more than two million in order to be any sort of actual investment.

Now, you could say it’s investment in quality of life, you could say it’s investment in having a roof over our heads, but I consider it consumer debt simply because we decide the size, the location, we decide all of the things about the house that make the house cost what it costs and require us to take on the amount of debt that we take on. And those are all consumer decisions. Unless again, you’re like actually investing in real estate, you’re typically making consumer decisions for a house that you want to live in.

I think this is very important because in society, we have created a norm, a normality of high consumer debt when it comes to housing. It’s like, yeah, this is just a normal thing. We have $700,000 of debt or, you know, even more. Like whatever it is, it’s like it becomes this normal thing to have hundreds of thousands of dollars of consumer debt because of the choices of where we want to live and how many rooms we want to have and the type of square footage we want and the type of land that we want with it and how many the fancy things come with it or what do we want it to look like? All of those things factor in, and we’re totally fine with them, and we have typically very little thoughts about them. We’re like, yeah, this is just what you do. This is actually a sign of success that I have this debt.

It’s very fascinating, but it’s something to notice because when you are an entrepreneur, you really are living outside of the societal norm in how you think in a lot of the ways that you will have to decision-make. And so one of the things that I would always suggest to people when they start a business is you want to get your consumer spending down as much as possible.

I’m not saying sell your house. I’m just saying you want to get consumer spending down as much as possible because there will need to be investments in your business. And I’ve seen a lot of people have a really high consumer lifestyle that then requires the business to pay for that consumer lifestyle.

So then they get in business debt, and then they blame the debt instead of taking responsibility and ownership for their consumer spending. Right? Like if you are making $100,000 or $200,000 and you get your nails done and your hair did and you, you know, have like you a certain wardrobe style that you have to wear and you only like to take certain vacations and you like to go out to certain restaurants and you have like this lifestyle that you’re paying for. Well, that’s not really on the business. That’s not the business isn’t performing to match your lifestyle. It’s that your lifestyle isn’t matching the performance of the business. And that’s a really important thing to know.

Okay? So, knowing that, the way that I think about investment debt, I hold two things true at the same time. I now grow a business that it is debt-free. I build a very lean business that is built on the profit, reinvesting the profit of the business. So after we pay all of our expenses, the profit we have, then some of that goes to me, and some of that gets reinvested in the business for future success. And that’s how I fund the growth of my business. And that is one of my biggest values in my business is having a cash flow positive business and being very lean in how I grow so that I don’t have to take on big amounts of business debt in order to grow.

However, when I started, I had no personal startup capital to truly invest in order to get my business off the ground. So I did have to take on debt in order to grow my business. And in the beginning, it was consumer debt in the sense that it was on my personal credit card. Then I got a business credit card, and it went on the business credit card, but, and it was still, I was still writing it off as a business expense, but in the end, I still had to use debt to grow my business. And so it’s really tricky for me to tell people not to have ever go into debt. Don’t take out a, you know, a PayPal loan, or don’t get a new credit card, or don’t ask for a credit line extension.

It’s hard for me to be an integrity to say that and to say it’s bad and that you should build a cash flow positive business from the very beginning and never take on debt, and debt is bad, because I had to leverage debt in order to grow my business. That is my story. And I leveraged debt, not a ton, but I did leverage at least ten grand at a time of debt, if not a little bit more, to grow my business all the way up until I think $100,000. Maybe it was like $100,000… the year I made $150,000, I just remember still having about twelve-ish thousand dollars of debt and then I just remember that next year around $300k is when I feel like maybe I stopped having to do that.

However, I will say, there were other times where I had to get really tricky when we bought our house. I did have a client that I coached recently who had a multimillion-dollar business, like an eight-figure, ten-million-dollar business. And she got into business debt towards the end of the business, and then fell out of love with the business.

She ended up paying off the debt, but then closed the business, and then she became a coach. And as she became a coach and she’s building up her business, a bank offered her a line of credit. And she took it. And we were exploring the reasons why she took it, but essentially, what we learned is that she, in the first debt, it was because she wouldn’t let employees go. She felt responsible for them. And so she went into debt herself, being responsible for other people. And then the second time, she realized, I take on the debt and I use the line of credit instead of figuring out how to sell more because it’s more comfortable.

So as long as I have the ability to take the debt on, I will, and I won’t force myself to do the uncomfortable thing, or I won’t coach myself to do the uncomfortable thing, to not need to take on the debt, to just create the money. And I do think a lot of us do that. Like one of the things we talked about in Return On Investment is a lot of people leave returns on the table because they’re just unwilling to do the uncomfortable thing that they would need to do, or feel the uncomfortable thing, or think the uncomfortable thing while they’re in an investment container. They don’t do it. They don’t show up. They don’t participate. They don’t lean in. They don’t belong. Right? They don’t choose to get the return to extract the value because it’s more uncomfortable.

They’re actually more uncomfortable trying to extract the value and show up as the person who gets the result versus taking on the debt. It’s actually just easier for them to take on the debt. And then they can shame themselves about the debt instead of shaming themselves for possibly failing if they do the thing. Our brains are like, y’all, they’re all crazy. Like we’re just not wired for, we have to really, really have to rewire the basic functions of our brains. They all do this. It’s like a lot of nonsense, like taking action that makes no sense.

So it’s really powerful if you’re in debt and you’re resisting it, you could ask what you learned from it. Did you take on an investment that you didn’t actively engage to create an ROI? Did you take on an investment that you expected to do the work for you, and you didn’t do the work? Did you take on an investment that you ignored red flags within yourself and said yes, even though there was red flags coming up, but you decided I’m not as expert as this other person, so I’m going to pay them, and I’m going to hope that their expertise rubs off on me and then you don’t make the money back. Did I, was I afraid to let go of employees? I just couldn’t do it.

You want to really evaluate so that you don’t repeat it if it feels like something that isn’t in benefit of you. Like if you take on debt to invest in your business and then you create a return, you’re not going to be bothered by that. So if you’re bothered by the debt, you want to learn from it, so you don’t repeat it in the same way.

And then something else to think about, which I’ve already said, is what if this is a more common problem than you think, and you’re not a personal failure? 70% of businesses have debt right now. So if you have it, you’re part of the 70%. Now, I know it doesn’t make it better for you, but I think it’s interesting to know that it’s a more common problem than you think.

Now, I bet 70% of those businesses are, like I’m wonder what the percent of that 70% is startup businesses, but even if it’s to maintain the asset that’s going to pay you forever, it doesn’t mean you’re a personal failure. It means you’re an entrepreneur. And you do what it takes to create the asset and keep it alive so that you can profit for years and years to come so that you don’t have to work for someone else. That’s the risk, the inherent risk of entrepreneurship. That’s what we do.

So here’s, I created like a little bit of a process, like a four-step process, if you have debt that I wanted to share with you. It’s very simple, but it’s very powerful. You want to first find allowance for how much debt you have and how long you will be in it. That’s the first step.

The second step is to create a plan for payoff that doesn’t include starving yourself or the business. Or doesn’t require urgency or being rushed. So, notice if your plan for payoff requires urgency, rushed, starving yourself, or starving the business. It’s going to be really hard to pay that debt off if you’re starving the business, because you can pay the debt by starving the business and then having like not investing, not having any sort of business expenses, like you could do that, but you’ll and you’ll be paying it slowly because you’ll just be paying it off of the profit that you have after starving your business.

Or you could invest in your business, figure out what’s happening that’s keeping you from making more money to pay off that debt, and then maybe you make so much more money that you’re able to easily pay off the debt. Like that’s another option other than starving the business. Like the year that I didn’t take a profit, I also invested $233,000 in the business. And in that year, I took my restructured business that had a profit of like maybe 10% all the way to 65% in the middle of the restructuring. Like that’s profound.

But if I had just like been like, I got to do it on my own and I can’t have any support and I can’t have any help and I can’t get any, you know, mindset help, business help, marketing help, like I don’t know that I would have gone to 65% profit at the multimillion dollar level. It’s crazy. In twelve months. So, like between this year and next year, I’m probably going to make up for the year that I didn’t take the profit and how profitable we are. It’s bananas.

So, create a plan for payoff that doesn’t, my advice is that doesn’t include starving yourself or the business, and it doesn’t require urgency or being rushed. And starving yourself is not the same as cutting your luxury consumer lifestyle. Just so you know, that’s not the same. Starving yourself means actually not allowing yourself to live any joy or any have anything at all because you’re so shamed for having debt. We don’t want to do that, but we also want to look at, could I cut things down?

Then the third step is you want to enroll your financial partners in your plan. So your spouse or your business partner in your plan and set boundaries. Now, this is where I could see myself getting in trouble because if your spouse is listening to this episode, and I tell like, what I’m going to advise you is to tell your spouse, this is my plan, this is how long it’s going to take to get the business, the debt paid off and the business back to health, and until it’s there, I can’t, this is either I can’t put money towards the family living expenses or this is the only amount of money I can put towards the family living expenses and it’s final.

Because we have to keep the asset. And it’s hard because you’re the person not building the business that isn’t the CEO, doesn’t understand what it’s going to take for you to manage your mind with the debt, and go out and keep making money. Like it’s a superhuman thing, especially if you have a lot of it. So then go out and figure out how to make enough money to pay that off, plus then some, because you want to pay yourself. And so you can’t have someone nagging you about how much debt you have, how long you’ve had that debt, when’s it going to be paid off? What’s happening with the business? Why aren’t you making more money? None of that is helpful.

So you really have to set boundaries around letting other people shame you, other people rush you, other people put pressure on you. You can’t allow it. It will crumble you when it comes to making money. And if you are a partner listening to this episode with your spouse who maybe has investment or business debt, just know that I’m on your side. I want your partner to get out of the debt as well. I want your partner to have a healthy business that pays for all of your expenses. Of course.

It’s my dream when businesses start paying for vacations and start paying for retire spouses and pay for private schools, and buy new homes. I love that. But I also know that CEOs can’t operate very well under pressure and urgency and shame and regret and someone else pushing them and making them feel terrible. It’s not going to, it’s not going to help them sell coaching.

So you’ve got to enroll your financial partners in your plan, and you’ve got to set boundaries. And then you’ve got to execute the plan with confidence, sufficiency, and worthiness. You are not your debt. Your value is not decreased because of your debt. Your leadership is not in question because of your debt. Your money-making capacity is only influenced by your debt if you allow it. I really want you to hear that.

And lastly, you get to decide how you want to feel about it. In fact, the way I like to feel, like think about debt, that creates a really positive feeling for me is that debt can be your silent partner. It can be what allows you to create your business and your freedom. It can be what keeps you holding on to your asset. It can provide opportunities you wouldn’t normally have access to. Now, it should be used intentionally with awareness to the risk, with tolerance to the risk, and commitment to honor it.

So I want to tell you one last story because we also live in a society where we are constantly looking to get out of owning and being responsible for things. We want to blame other people, we want to get out of things, we don’t want to honor things because it’s easier. So in college, I had a friend who filed for bankruptcy, and we had the exact same amount of debt, like roughly $10,000 to $12,000. She filed for bankruptcy, and I did a debt management program.

And here was the thought I had that had me do that debt management program, that has now become such a valuable story and a way I coach my clients that I’ve made so much money from that experience of having that. Like it’s part of my value that I now deliver as a coach is having gone through that experience. My thought at the time, without ever having a coach and knowing what coaching was, because I had the, I mean, my friend’s parents were really close to me, so they were urging me to file bankruptcy. They were like, then you won’t have to pay it off, and you can start fresh. Then you don’t have, you know, you don’t have to spend years trying to make it work.

But my thought was, I spent this money, I agreed to pay this money, I owe it, and it’s my lesson to pay it. I thought that before I even became a coach. I just felt like it would be wrong to file bankruptcy. I chose to go into the boutiques. I chose to try on the clothes. I chose to buy the clothes. I chose to go out to the restaurants. I chose to go out to the clubs at the time. I’m not doing that stuff now. I chose to go on the trips. I chose to rack the money up. I chose to live above my expenses. And I signed every credit card slip saying I’m paying that money. I owe it.

And I really believed it would be a great lesson for me to figure out how to pay it. I just knew it. I knew something inside of me, if I learn how to pay this, it’s going to it’s going to mean something. If I pay this off, I’m going to know this about myself that I pay my debts. Like that is my self-concept. I pay my contracts, I pay my debts, I pay what’s owed. And because I know that about myself, I can sleep really well at night. Like, I feel very good about myself at night.

And I do think it’s important for us, when at all possible, if at all possible, to pay the debt, to figure it ou,t and to learn the lesson because if you learn the lesson, then you get to keep the value forever, and then the value goes into the asset. Right? This experience for you will then become something you coach someone on at some point, or something similar. And you will coach them like a rock star straight through it, and you will become so valuable that more people will want to pay you, and you’ll make more and more money.

So it can be your silent partner that allows you to create your business and your freedom, that keeps you holding on to your asset, that provides opportunities you wouldn’t normally have access to. And you are not the number of your debt. Your value hasn’t decreased. Your leadership is not in question. And it only impacts your ability to make money if you allow it.

All right. I hope this episode was so helpful. I’ve been thinking about it for so long and just wanting to have a conversation with all of you about business debt and I just, if anything, want to make you all have better, more useful thoughts so that you can go out and make money and then obviously get out of the debt and grow your financial asset of your business for years and years to come. I’m on your side with this, I promise. I hope you all have the best, most amazing week, and I will talk to you next week.

Hey, if you’re ready to make money as a life coach, I want to invite you to join my 2K for 2K program; where you’re going to make your first $2,000 the hardest part using my simple five-step formula for getting consults and closing new clients. Just head over to StaceyBoehman.com/2Kfor2K. We’ll see you inside.

title: Ep #343: Investing Shame, Blame, and Regret
transcript:
Welcome
 to the 
Make Money as a Life Coach
®
 
podcast
 
where sales expert and Master Coach Stacey Boehman teaches you how to make your first $2K, $20K, and $200K using her proven formula.

Hey coaches, welcome to Episode 343. Today, we’re going to talk about investment shame, blame, and regret. So this was one of the topics in the ROI, Return on Investment, Entrepreneur Series course that we just finished up. And it was one of the most powerful calls that we had. We actually talked about this over our final two calls. And I wanted to share some of the things I taught the students and some of the coaching that I gave the students that I wanted to really just pass on to everyone, even if you, you know, didn’t join the course. I think everyone needs to hear this message.

And I delivered it very differently in the ROI training, the energy, the way I was able to build up and lay out the foundation was really beautiful, and it was a very loving, compassionate message. And this one, I want it to be a little more empowered and a little stronger, also for the students that were in that course, to have like another take at this.

So, this is what we’re going to dive into today. So here’s one of the things that I shared with my students that I think you need to know. Shame, when it comes to anything, but we’re going to have this conversation around investing, shame keeps us from wisdom. We trade wisdom for shame. We don’t realize we’re doing that, but that is what happens when we allow ourselves to feel shame, then we aren’t open to the wisdom that we could learn and the value that we could extract from the thing that’s creating the shame.

And blame keeps us from responsibility and empowerment. And one of the things I always say when it comes to responsibility is the definition that I love to think about is the ability to respond to any situation or the ability to respond in any situation. So it’s not, “it’s my fault.” It’s, “if I take responsibility, then I have the ability to respond in any situation with what I’m going to do, how I’m going to react, how I’m going to move forward, the value I’m going to extract from something, the empowerment I’m going to choose to step up into.”

And blame keeps us from that. It keeps us disempowered and not responsible. So we also miss the wisdom from blame. And regret really keeps us stuck in the past, wishing to change it, but without the energy to actually make the change because regret feels so heavy that we don’t have any energy to even do anything about it. We just spin in our head, thinking about wishing we could change the past, and why did we do that, and shoulding ourselves and shaming ourselves on top of the regret. And really, it has us very past-focused and in our emotional world. Like our emotions get stuck in that past experience that we created regret with.

Instead of getting the wisdom by taking the responsibility and the empowerment and then gaining energy to be able to actually utilize the value that you learn from every situation that goes unexpected to make a change, including every investment that you make. So, having investment shame blocks your wisdom from learning anything from that investment. The blame keeps you from being responsible and empowered and learning for you how to be a better investor and how to respond to any situation as an investor, and regret keeps you fearing bad investments and in the emotion of not getting what you wanted from the investment, and then not really having the energy to be able to learn and grow as an investor and then go create bigger returns in the future with new investments.

So the biggest ones that we coached on were shame and regret. Those are the ones as people came up to be coached, those are the two emotions that typically my students presented with. They presented with shame for money spent without a return, shame for leaving a full-time job, and expecting to make money or replace their income faster. Shame for not being able to support their family with their business. Shame for lifestyles having to be simplified because they aren’t making as much money as they expected or that they didn’t make enough money back from investments, enough profit on top of investments to also live the lifestyle they want to live and invest in their business.

Shame for being stuck on the same issue in investing for a long time, like buying coaching over and over and over to solve a thing that never gets solved. Shame for failure, for not getting returns, for not learning the lessons, for not implementing things that you purchased. Regret for investment decisions with coaches, regret for over investing, buying too many things, and regret for expecting the investment to do the work, and realizing that after the fact, and not getting the return.

They also presented with regret for not stewarding their money wiser, for not showing up to investments, for not using their time wisely in investments, for not doing the work. But remember, shame and regret keep you stuck in the emotion of what happened without the power to learn from it and do something about it. They let us indulge in self-loathing rather than self-compassion, and again, responsibility and empowerment. They keep us hidden instead of visible.

Shame and regret also leave you trying to change the past in your mind or feeling so bad about what happened so that you don’t repeat it in the future. It’s like, let me make myself feel so terrible because that I need to feel this terrible to learn not to repeat it. But then we get stuck in the feeling that terrible, and it doesn’t have you focused on creating for the future. You can literally drown yourself in shame until you become invisible.

Or you can extract value from the lesson that the shame and the regret is here to teach you. And you can move forward empowered and wiser than before. Questions you can ask yourself are, what’s here for me to learn? What’s the wisdom that I can gain here? How can I extract value from this experience? Good or bad, how can I extract value as an investor from this experience? What can I learn about myself as an investor here?

And really dive in. There’s a lot that can be learned here that can empower you to move forward instead of having you feel stuck in the shame and in the regret. And there’s a lot of possible lessons that you can learn from these questions and from this shame and this regret and all the different ways that it shows up. But a few of them that I offered to my students through our Facebook community and coaching on the posts, and through the coaching that happened on the calls, and through the teaching.

One of them is that the lesson sometimes that we need to learn is that we have growth entitlement. So we make our best guess, our best theory for how long it will take to create a business and make steady money or replace income, and we decide that’s how it should be. That’s the right answer. And then we feel entitled to that result in that time frame. And how we know we feel entitled is that we think something has gone wrong when it doesn’t work out that way.

We shame ourselves for not doing it in our arbitrary timeline that we chose that is often missing the wisdom of what it really takes to make it. Like, I thought I was going to leave my job. I got certified in March of 2015 and I thought I would leave my job by June. That was my expectation. That was my entitlement. I didn’t leave until the following September. That was the real wisdom of what it took to make my business work and to create $100,000.

And then in our upset and shame, we take ourselves out of learning and responsibility, and doing the hard work. And we spend time instead being defeated instead of triumphing. Right? You spend your time worrying instead of theorizing and evaluating. This is the biggest one. Of everybody I spoke to, they’re spending their time in the shame and the regret and the blame and the worry instead of their time spent theorizing and evaluating and going again. And that is what it takes to be successful.

I don’t care how you get there. You’ve got to get there. If you want to be successful, you have to be in the cycle of theorizing. What are my top three theories as to why this didn’t work? That doesn’t include somebody else, that doesn’t include blame, that allows me to be responsible and empowered. What are my top three theories of what I did, how I showed up, why I didn’t get what I came for? What worked? What didn’t work? What am I going to do differently? And then going again, and again, and again, and learning from each and every single thing we do and every single investment we make.

But instead, you spend time fighting against what is right now in this moment, instead of creating what could be from the lessons, from the wisdom, from the empowerment, from the responsibility. And you really do need 100% of your energy going to figure out what is working and what isn’t working and what you need to do differently. You need 100% of your energy in creating new beliefs and new skill sets in marketing and selling your offer, in getting results for yourself and then for your clients.

So all of the shame and the regret is just it’s sucking all of your time and your energy and making you think the business doesn’t work when really the emotions aren’t working to create the business. And the truth is, your biggest source of shame may be coming from a thought error. I saw this one a lot. My students believe their business should be supporting their family, paying their bills. And before $100,000, it absolutely should not be. And I know that’s a truth that maybe you don’t want to hear.

And really, even before $200k, I wouldn’t be expecting too much of it. I think it takes $200k to live well now in this current world, in this current economy, and invest in your business to grow it, pay your taxes. That’s what it takes. So I would have the goal of $200k or go home. Like, honestly. If you had someone else, you know, working and you didn’t require of your business, if it was like a side business, of course, you could make $40k, $60k, $100k and be very, very happy. But to actually like pay your family’s bills, and especially depending on where you live, you want to get to $200k as fast as possible because that’s where it can really start doing that.

Maybe even $300k. Again, can you live off of it beforehand? Yes. You can live off your business at $100k, before $100k, but will it be at the expense of not growing as fast and making more money in the future? Likely. Which is why I kept my full-time job until I made $100k. And even then, after I left my job at $100k, it was dicey between $100k and $300k to invest in my business in the way that I wanted to, to grow it as fast as I wanted to grow, to go where I was going and also pay my own bills. And it was just me. I didn’t have kids, I didn’t have a family. It was just me.

So if you try to live off of it beforehand, and I understand some people do end up in situations where they have to. And if you are that person, then you can’t feel regret about it should be different. You’ve got to just move forward with this is what it is. And I’ve got to figure out how to stay in a cycle that keeps me moving forward and growing as fast as I can and I don’t have room for the shame and the blame and the regret.

But watch Shark Tank. Like, if you haven’t, I’ve seen so many seasons of that. The people who pay themselves big salaries and use the business’s profit to live off of and don’t work like a full-time job or even a part-time job while building the business, those people almost never get the deal because the Sharks don’t see them as like really wanting to grow aggressively and they’re only looking to invest in people wanting to grow aggressively.

Entrepreneurship is a huge lesson in delayed gratification. And I know delayed gratification does not feel good, but on the other side is a multiple six-figure business that could be paying for lots of things, lots of dream vacations, dream, you know, mortgages, like private schools, extracurricular activities, college educations. Like, there’s a lot on the line to be able to build a business that eventually can pay the bills.

Right? So if you want to succeed massively to where one day your business does provide solely for your family, it’s got to have time, money, and energy to grow. It needs to be treated like an asset for your future. No differently than your stock portfolio. Like, you wouldn’t put $100,000 into stocks and expect the dividends to start paying for your lifestyle each month immediately. But we do this with entrepreneurship from a thought error that it should be that way.

So the reality check might be the lesson in the wisdom. Oh, it’s harder than I thought. It’s going to take longer than I thought to pay the bills. I’m going to have to build it bigger than I thought. I didn’t realize this ahead of time. I’m going have to invest more than I anticipated so that I can grow my belief and my skill sets and become the person who can make that type of money quicker.

And I’ve said this many times to my students over the years and I know how painful it feels, but you may need to go back to work. If you left early and you thought it was going to grow faster, and it didn’t, and your family needs your income, you might have to go back to work, even if you don’t want to, for a little bit. Maybe a few years. In the scheme of things, if it you have to work for three more years in your full-time job in order to then have a business that can pay your family for the next 20 or 30 years, think of it relatively.

And it isn’t a sign of failure to have to go back to work. Right? So we don’t need to have shame about it. So many people have shame about it. I’m going back to work or I’m getting a part-time job, so I’m going to feel shame because I failed. No, it’s a sign of entrepreneurial and life maturity. And this is what I try to call people into. It’s really coming from the emotional capacity to handle setbacks. Like I can handle a setback. I can handle when things don’t go my way.

I’ve been so, like in my business in 10 years, there have been times where I’ve had to scale back my lifestyle. I’ve had to stop buying things, stop taking trips, stop doing things in order to invest in my business, or pay an unexpected tax bill, or hire more employees, or restructure the business. Like, there have been times like I just spent 18 months not taking a profit. I pay myself like a very minuscule salary. We ended up having to raise it based on our profit this year, but it was like not enough to pay our bills.

So for 18 months, we lived off of savings so that I could restructure my business and have freedom as a new mom in my business. And I believed like, I just treated my business as an asset. Like I’m doing this for 18 months and it’s going to be painful, but also at the same time, I’m going to create an asset that now works for my mom life and me for the next 10, 20, 30 years. I don’t know, however long I work.

We bought land to build a dream house, like a gigantic dream house, expecting my business before I had a baby to grow at the rate that it had for years prior, not expecting being a mom to impact my business and my revenue at all. And now we’re going to sell it. In the beginning, it felt like a setback initially, but because the wisdom came through of the business I really want to have and what it really requires at this level and that revenue isn’t guaranteed. Like that wisdom had me move in a completely different direction with no regrets.

In fact, I feel grateful for all the lessons I learned in the last three years that didn’t have me building a house that might have ended up creating extreme financial pressure for me that would have had me taken away from how much I want to spend with my kids because I’d always be worried about that mortgage. And instead, the wisdom has me aggressively investing my money into passive income streams and our stock portfolio, and places where our money can grow without me having to do the work, versus on real estate that I’m not even planning on using as an investment. I want to live there forever.

So if you find yourself in a scenario where you’ve had a lofty expectation of what could be and it isn’t, that is life. That is entrepreneurship. And it’s your time to get tough, not weak, to handle a setback, to find sufficiency, to create a new plan from wisdom. We’re still going to buy the dream house, but now that I know what kind of lifestyle that I want and what is my priority now financially for the future now with children and having the from desire of wanting my business to be highly profitable and for me to be highly happy and not stressed at all, we’re going to move that back a few years. It’s not a problem. I love the house we live in now.

It’s so crazy. I wanted to I remember I wanted a pool so bad. We almost had one put here, but our yard is just not quite big enough to like, our dogs wouldn’t have had anywhere to run around in, and so we decided not to. But I was feeling so sad that I didn’t have a pool, and I just wanted a pool so bad, and I imagined all the pool time I would spend with my kids. And now I’ve heard of like so many kids drowning recently. Like just my heart can’t handle it. And I told my husband the other day, I’m like, I’m so glad we don’t have a pool with young children.

Whether there would be a fence or a thing or anything, like I just don’t think I could handle the anxiety now that I’m a parent. Like, I’m glad we didn’t do that. I don’t need that until they’re they’re much older and they’re very proficient in swimming. So things happen. You postpone things, you change things, your wisdom shapes you differently.

Right? I have a new goal that my investments can pay the mortgage if they had to, permanently, or that I can easily pay cash for the house, or pay off the house in a few years, which is what we did with this house. But coming from the priority of I always put my business first, and sometimes this is the lesson. This is the wisdom that the shame and the regret and the blame need to teach you. Is did you put your business first in an investment you made? Did you protect your profit? I’ve had so many people come into investments, even with me, that I tell them, make sure you protect your profit, which means you keep selling what has been working and what has been selling while you think about building this other thing. Like, especially 2 Million Dollar Group students.

They’re so obsessed with scaling that they want to leave behind their previous business and just go straight to their scalable offer. And it’s like, no, no, no, the first year, you’ve got to protect your revenue and your profit with so if you made $200,000 or $300,000 last year with one-on-one in group, you do that while creating the scalable offer and then you set a goal that includes that income plus the money from the scalable offer. And then once that money matches the money from the previous offers, then you skyrocket that scalable offer.

And when you don’t put the business first like that, when you make a rash decision and you just jump into a new offer and you stop doing what’s working and you stop selling because you’re so excited to learn new things, that’s sometimes the lesson. You got to put your business, your profit, your revenue first. You’ve got to go into your investments deciding to make your money back right away so that you profit the rest of the time. You’ve got to, like I taught my students an ROI plan that helps them make sure that they don’t end up in a situation where their business isn’t put first.

And an ROI method to help them keep the business first and keep themselves as the responsible, empowered steward of the business. This may be the lesson. I treat my business like an asset that is going to be an asset for the rest of my life, not just today, and I treat myself as the CEO and the sole person responsible for its revenue, always. That might be the lesson. The lessons and the wisdom waiting for you could also be that you stewarded money before in a way that you didn’t love, and you learned. And it helped you become the version of you who will steward it better from here on out.

I coached someone on this, and it was so powerful. She kept telling herself she was irresponsible with money. And it’s like, no, it sounds like where you’re at now with the regret that you have, you’ve become very responsible. You’ve seen how you spent your money, and you didn’t like it. And you learned, and now you want to do it differently. And so for every dollar you make moving forward, you will. But only if you can get out of the regret. If you can see that you needed that to happen to become the person that doesn’t want to spend money that way and wants to spend it differently and is stewarding it in a very different capacity and is paying attention to it in a very different way.

But you’ve got to be future-focused from here on out. Right? Sometimes we can’t get to financial responsibility without going through a little irresponsibility. But you can’t get stuck there. You’ve got to learn. You can’t decide past mistakes mean you are incapable of learning and involving and becoming more savvy. If you haven’t used investments well, if you haven’t showed up the way that you wanted, if you haven’t done the work, and you know it, you know it’s on you, then why? What are your top three theories? Let’s grow from this, not wilt.

I know it’s painful to look, but it’s more painful not to look and to stay stuck. It’s more painful to never become the person with all the wisdom, to let the shame and the regret steal your dreams and your capacity and your capability to achieve them. And if you’re stressed about the time it’s taking, well, it takes more time to stress about it than to just get it done. So let’s do it. Like, let’s just do it with focus, 100% of it. Sit with the shame, look at it in the mirror, process it, and then let it go. Let the wisdom come through.

Now, the final thing I want to touch on is blame. Blame shields us from shame and regret. We don’t have to feel the shame and the regret, so it feels a little bit better when we can put it on someone else, then we don’t have to feel it ourselves. But the problem is, it eats you alive in the exact same way as shame and regret. Instead of making yourself the villain, which is what we do in shame and regret, you make someone else or something else the villain, but then you spend your time in a fight between good and evil.

You lead with either weakness as a victim or righteousness as the hero fighting the villain, and instead of wisdom and vulnerability as a leader. And it’s a very different energetic exchange there, a different energetic output that you’re putting into the world. And what it causes you to do is leave your lane to try to change the someone or the something, instead of staying in your lane, changing you. And you lose personal empowerment every single day that you blame someone or something else for your investments not going right or your results that you’ve created.

You start to subtly believe that other people and things control your outcomes, and you stop being the coach your clients need because now you’re wounded by coaching that you’ve bought. And it’s very hard to sell coaching powerfully from a wound, from disconnection, from righteousness. And if you do sell it, look out for the clients who respond to this. If they’re responding to your victim and not your empowerment, having a client base full of victims who also blame when they don’t get what they expected or desired, eventually, you become their villain.

Trade the blame for empowerment. Whether it’s your kids, your coach, your husband, your job, your colleagues, a program that you bought, the process that you were taught that you didn’t think worked, it’s all keeping you from learning something about you. That could be why you ignored red flags in yourself before you invested in something, why you didn’t trust yourself, why you believed gossip, and took yourself out of an investment that you needed and could have really benefited from.

You could learn from what was inside of you that was attracted to a coach who has wounds and villains. Were you waiting and expecting for the coach to do the work rather than implementing and owning your decisions and being the CEO? Like I told my students, I want you to think about this. I told them, I showed them, actually. I had them do an exercise. I showed them how it feels. But it feels like crap to truly be responsible and empowered, if you really think about it.

Because you have to give up the story keeping yourself disempowered, and look at yourself. And it feels confronting and hard and frustrating and isolating and triggering. But the result is feeling alive, triumphant, empowered, invincible, confident, equipped, energized, intelligent, free, grounded, connected, whole. Like the list goes on. That’s the result, the way you feel after empowerment and responsibility. But getting into empowerment and responsibility feels terrible.

But you’ve got to be willing to do it because on the other side truly is power and freedom. It’s a future that you want that you figure out how to create. And it’s you helping other people get out of their shame and regret and blame in their lives. Because if, think about it, if everybody walking around the world stopped indulging in shame and regret and blame, if they were able to process it and move through it, no matter, and I coached some people who are dealing with some really heavy shame. Really heavy shame for many years of their lives, like painful suffering.

But when you can let that go, holy smokes, the energy that you have, the power that you have to move your life forward to what you want is going to be incredible. It’s totally worth it.

Okay. That’s my message, folks. I love you. I believe in you. I am here to support you. Try letting this go. Try working through this. Try not letting this eat you alive. You deserve to have the business and the entrepreneur experience that you want and that you’ve dreamed of. But it just can’t include these three things.

And if you missed ROI or any of the Entrepreneur Series courses to date, stay tuned. People have been asking. There were students in ROI asking about Capacity Work and Served. There were people emailing in trying to get in ROI after we closed the doors. And we really meant it, so we did, we did keep the doors closed. But stay tuned. Keep your eyes open. Make sure you’re getting my emails and they’re not going to your promotions tab.

Make sure that you’re following the correct @StaceyBoehman on Instagram and Facebook. There’s a lot of fake accounts rolling around right now. We try to get them shut down quickly, but mine is the blue check mark. That’s how you know. I have the blue check mark. But there is an opportunity coming, so I want you to be prepared for it. All right. Have a beautiful week. I love you all. Talk to you next week.

Hey, if you’re ready to make money as a life coach, I want to invite you to join my 2K for 2K program; where you’re going to make your first $2,000 the hardest part using my simple five-step formula for getting consults and closing new clients. Just head over to StaceyBoehman.com/2Kfor2K. We’ll see you inside.

title: Ep #342: Being On the Fence and How to Get Off
transcript:
Welcome
 
to the 
Make Money as a Life Coach
®
 
podcast
 
where sales expert and Master Coach Stacey Boehman teaches you how to make your first $2K, $20K, and $200K using her proven formula.

Hey coaches, welcome to episode 342. Today, we’re going to talk about being on the fence and how to get off for you as the student, and then for your clients, and why this matters. So I have been, this year, if you haven’t noticed, selling a lot.

Now, part of that, the biggest part of that, is that I started this year as my 10th year in business, my celebration year. And I have, for the last two years, I think I’ve talked about this on the podcast, that I have been creating courses in my Notes app on my phone. Like this idea for a course, this idea for a course, paying attention to my students, but I never had the energy, the time, and there were other things in the business that needed worked on that I couldn’t put that work out into the world. And then we finally got to a place where I could just unleash value, unleash creativity, play, just launch.

And so I have, I think, launched something almost every single, I think every single month this entire year so far. Now, part of that is also because I’m going on maternity leave, but I also wonder, I think if I weren’t going on maternity leave, there would just be something that we would be doing in August, September, and October as well. I feel on fire, my creativity is at the highest, and I’m just enjoying myself so much. I know so many people are afraid of launching, and they think it’s so masculine and it takes so much energy and it wears them out, but I have really had a lot of fun.

And one of the things that has happened this year, when because I’ve been selling more, is that when I sell, and I teach this to my students, is you’ve got to get people talking. It’s the number one thing. Your sales emails, your live streams, your social media posts, your, you know, networking, anything that you’re saying to market and sell your business is your best theories and your take on what you’re offering. And then there’s how people respond to it and what their thoughts are and what they’re looking for and so every time I do an entrepreneur series course, one of the things that’s been fascinating to me is the very first post when we open the group is always “tell me why you joined.” What about this marketing enticed you? What do you want to take away from this course?

And then, of course, what I love to do is then weave in the things that people say that aren’t in like the master curriculum. I weave those things in throughout the conversations to make sure people get what they came for and that we really touch on the way people experience, for example, how they experience lack of capacity or how they experience challenges in their business, or we’re doing ROI right now. So, you know, when they think of returns on investment, what inspired them and what do they want to take from that, and making sure that we really include… the conversation is robust.

And one of the other things that comes up a lot when I’m selling is the reasons people would and wouldn’t buy, right? When I’m getting people talking, that’s my goal. What are the reasons you would buy and you wouldn’t buy? Beyond “I’m not interested.” That’s not interesting. That’s not feedback that is really valuable, but to have someone tell you, this is what really drew me in, this is what felt valuable to me, or this is where I’m stuck, is really valuable information for you to help your people.

And so I’ve been selling a lot, and I naturally, as you sell more, you will also get more yeses, and then you will also get more no’s. This is something important to just know ahead of time. People think it’s one of the things, especially in my 2 Million Dollar Group, when we’re coaching, they’re so surprised when they start scaling, is how they feel like they’re getting more no’s than ever, and they are. But I always tell them, and you’re also making more money than ever.

We have to keep that in check, right? We have to know that just if you are offering a thousand people something and then 2,000 people and then 3,000 people, the more people you offer, the more there will be no’s, and also the more there will be yeses.

So the no’s, I like to study those and I like to think about them for my own self and my own marketing, but also for my teaching because I’m, it always feels like a meta experience, if that’s the right word for it, because I’m teaching you how to also sell to your people and you’re also a student buying from me.

So I always think there’s a lot to learn there. And so that’s really where this podcast is coming from is I’ve been getting of the group of no’s that I get, of people who talk to me during my sales sequence on the fence. Like “I’m on the fence of buying this thing,” “I’m on the fence of investing in this thing” has come up a lot.

And then in the coaching that I’m always doing, I’ve also found this coming up with being on the fence of actually building your business, being on the fence of quitting, being on the fence of going to the networking event, being on the fence of, you know, really going for it. Whatever it is, I just feel like in the last so far this year, the number one thing I’ve heard from a lot of people is that they’re on the fence. Like if they’re actually considering something, not “I’m not interested,” or “I’m a no,” or “I know that’s not for me,” but “I’m on the fence.” I do think that is an interesting thing to look at for my students who are also selling coaching to other people who may also be on the fence.

And I want to talk about this in a way that I think is really interesting, that I think maybe you haven’t thought about before of what being on the fence means that I if you stay with me could be a really big transformation for how you make decisions and then how you help other people make decisions. Because I do believe, and I’ve said this many times, if you’re in my 2k for 2k, you have heard me say this, our job as coaches, and it doesn’t matter what you coach on, health, nutrition, marriage, trauma, grief, divorce, weight loss, business, I mean, all of the different things. Whatever you coach on, at the end of the day, you are helping your clients make decisions that align with getting the results that they want.
