Then I wanna be thinking about long-term in my business, how many people I wanna be introducing to my business and nurturing in my business, and closing in my business today, every single day when I show up to market. I’m not thinking about, oh, there’s only two people watching me. That feels terrible. Or, oh, I need to like start running ads in order to grow my audience, and that’s the only way it grows.

No, I believe every day, without me doing anything, there is an audience that is available right now of all five types of those buyers, and they are different versions of cold, warm, and hot. And my job is to believe they are there, even if I don’t see them, because remember, 90%, if I focus on the 90%, it’s gonna look like there’s nobody there. But my job is to laser in on the people that could be there and serve them today, but show up big enough that I’m also bringing in people for the future. Because I know that it takes anywhere from one day to three years.

So if I, for example, am marketing my 200k Mastermind, I’m not showing up just for the sales and the amount of students I wanna work with tomorrow. I’m thinking about the next 12 months, the next 18 months. I’m thinking every time, I only sell it twice a year. So if I wanna have ultimate bigger brand awareness to reach early majority people and late majority people, I have to show up like I wanna sell to 1,000 people, even though that’s not actually how many people I’m going to be working with right now. But I wanna think about that. Like, what would I do? How big would I, how much value would I give? How big would I launch? What would I do differently if I knew that today’s marketing efforts were an investment for tomorrow?

And then I wanna think every single day, because I only launch twice a year, I wanna be thinking about how do I constantly be nurturing that audience? So one of the things I do is I email my waitlist every week. I have students come on the podcast and share what they’ve learned and how they created money and try to extract all of their knowledge while they’re in the flow of it. I talk about the concepts on the podcast. I talk about it on my social media.

I’m constantly serving my people. We’ll talk about that on Thursday. We’ll talk about delivering, but I’m thinking about serving the people now becomes, like their experience becomes what the late majority and the laggards need in order for them to buy. They need to have had a group of people that go through the process and do really well. And then I wanna stay out of any type of marketing despair. I wanna be like really well-coached in my brain.

This requires a lot of emotional intelligence, a lot of emotional regulation. talking about this in a lot of my containers lately, but the ability to hold hard feelings in your body because it’s your brain’s natural response, especially because of the way the algorithm is set up. If you’re interacting on social media, not all my clients do, but it’s a free platform for billions of people. So a lot of people are on social media, and the algorithm is just not set up to show us this 10% very easily, and to see and believe that they’re there right away.

So it requires a big amount of emotional regulation and being willing to hold hard things. And then increasing your capacity to be seen more and more so that you can reach more and more of the market, right? The more you’re able to show up consistently and give value, I call that recurring marketing is just marketing that your people can count on, places your people can count on.

So people can always count on a Monday email from me. If they’re on my 200k wait list, they can count on a Wednesday email from me. My people can count on a free podcast every Wednesday morning at 6 a.m. Most mornings, unless I got it in late, and then sometimes it’s 7 a.m. But every day, there’s never been a Wednesday that hasn’t had a podcast go by. They can count on me showing up on social media, not every day, but they can always say, like if I go to Stacey’s social media, I will see something inspiring. I will see something that is very specific to her work. I will see her talking about her work. I know it’s there.

So that’s like recurring marketing people can rely on, and I’m gonna be working on making sure I’m the type of person who delivers that no matter what’s happening in my life. It just happens. We get it done. We figure it out. Doesn’t matter if it was hard. Doesn’t matter if it was inconvenient. Doesn’t matter if it, whatever it is, it’s like I figure out how to do that. Sometimes that’s doing it ahead of time. Sometimes that’s meeting my own limiting beliefs and getting it done. There’s a lot of different things that happen, but I make sure people can start to rely on me.

Then we start calling people in with special event marketing, which are things like this. We’re like, here, come in and have an opportunity to engage with me with closer proximity, to get to know me, my brand, and what I offer on a closer level. And then let me, as I’m out on social media, and as I’m in these trainings, and as I’m coaching my people, demonstrate the emotional energy, the feelings that represent my brand. So you’ll always see me showing up grounded. You’ll always see me showing up thoughtful. You’ll always see me being very precise. And I’m very compelled all of the time for the work that we’re all doing as coaches. So I emulate that in all of my marketing. People feel that, and it makes sense for my brand.

And then the last thing that’s the part of the advanced selling philosophy is believing in demand, believing that there are people out there right now, not new people you have to go find, but people right now in your world, this just a small group of them, and your job is to get through to them. But they are there, they demand your work, and the more you get good at getting through to them, the bigger that audience gets.

That’s what we think about. That’s if we align our thinking, and that’s the way that we start operating on a daily basis, I want you to think about what a difference that would make in your business. If that’s the way you’re thinking, if that’s your normal set of standard belief systems. And then within that, these are the actions we take. These are the processes that we do.

So one of the things I teach in marketing that I think is very different from everybody else is that we work to close the existing audience we have first. It’s the most essential thing that you can do. It’s actually the least, like the way you can capitalize on your effort and your capacity, and it actually does change your problem-solving if that’s what you’re focused on instead of going out and getting new leads all the time. Going out and getting new leads comes from either not having the ability to close and give the people that are in the early and late majority what they need to buy, not knowing how to communicate with them, or it comes from being focused on the 90%.

And then thinking, obviously, disengagement means it’s not the right formula, so it’s not the right people, I have to go out and get more people, instead of I have to increase my skill at communicating with the people that already exist. I have to increase the value that I give to the people who already exist. So that’s the first most important thing.

Then the other thing that people would not expect, especially after you’ve listened to me talk about these five different types of buyers, is you actually wanna have a very simple marketing plan. Just like you wanna have a simple offer, you wanna have a really simple marketing plan. Here’s why. I have people even in my 2 Million Dollar Group who will tell me they are literally everywhere doing everything. It becomes very hard.

Michelle, I love this question. “How do you know your 10%?” It becomes very hard to figure out the answer to that question when you’re everywhere. When you’re on Instagram, when you’re on Facebook, when you’re on TikTok, when you’re on LinkedIn, when you’re running Google ads, when you’re on different job platforms, when you’re doing all of the things, all of the places, it becomes very, very difficult to know where people are coming from, what’s actually working. And then within that, you typically show up a little different with all of these platforms. So what’s that? How’s that working? And who are your actual people?

So you wanna have a very simple, essential marketing plan that allows you to really look at each place you’re showing up and really hone in on the 10% there. And you won’t always know your 10%. That’s the point. You have to believe that they’re there, even if they don’t show themselves to you.

I’ve said that, I’ve told this story many times, but every time I launch my 200k Mastermind, and this next launch will be my 12th or my 13th launch, but I always run a social media campaign. And really anytime I’m selling, but really specifically with this room, I see this a lot. If you went to my social media, and you can even scroll down and see the old launches, if you went there and you looked at the posts, and then you looked at the engagement, you would think this girl makes no money. There’s like six likes, two comments, sometimes no comments. And yet I would make 3 or 4 million dollars every time I launched the program, and have a lot, and I’ve served 700 students in the last 12 rounds.

So it’s not evident that you see them. They don’t typically show themselves. The buyers that actually buy, they don’t typically tell you they’re buying in the comments. They don’t typically share it to their story. They don’t typically engage because they’re buying. And then on top of that, it’s like, it’s just our expectation with the way social media runs that we’re gonna post, and the 10% are just gonna reveal themselves.

No, that’s actually the hard work of advanced marketing. It’s the belief in demand. You have to believe that 10% is there. You have to believe that as a circumstance, as a truth of the world, without seeing any evidence. And then you have to show up to speak to the,m regardless of what it looks like, regardless of anything. And then you use the feedback to just improve constantly. So it’s not that you do the same thing over and over, but you do improve over and over.

One of the best questions I ask myself in my marketing to improve is, what else haven’t I said? What can I say that I haven’t said? What’s a different angle I can take? I think about the types of buyers, and I think, let me write an email. Let me write an email specifically for them. Let me make a post directly for them. And I make sure I’m covering all of them. I think about the people who are hot right now, and I speak to them. I think about the people who are warm. What’s their tipping point? What might they need to hear?

Then I think about cold and I make sure that even though I speak with familiarity because I know people have been following me for years, I also speak as if no one’s ever heard about my offers. I speak as if they’re brand new and I don’t assume that anyone has heard a podcast or anyone’s read a previous email or anyone’s done a previous thing. And I’m able to focus on that because there’s a simple marketing plan.

The third step of the advanced selling process is overselling, and the way that I want you to think about it for this specific training is it’s over-giving value. A lot of times we think about, if I wanna close 10 people in my group, I’m gonna give value thinking about those 10 people. But we underestimate the amount of effort, energy, value that we have to give to close 10 people. So we’ve gotta do way more. We’ve gotta think about how many people do I wanna sell in a year? How many people do I wanna sell in three years? And then I need to show up to give that value right now.

And then the fourth step is I really want to work to create content specifically meant to speed up my client’s buy cycle, to figure out what needs to be said, what type of value I need to give, what do they need to believe in order to be ready to buy right now.

These are each things that we could spend an hour talking about each and every single one of these things, but I just want you to know that these are tools at your disposal that make focusing on the 10% a lot more productive and easier and increase the value every single time you show up when you work on these things.

So the fifth thing, and I’ve already mentioned this, but I actively spend time solving for what I think each buyer type needs. So when I create a launch, when I create a marketing sequence or a sales sequence, I’m always thinking, everyone’s like, how do you create so many emails at once? And what do you put in your emails? But what I put in my emails are just me thinking about those five buyer types and how can I address all of them? How can I make sure I touch on each thing, something that would be important for each of them?

And then this is the most important. People buy based on energy, based on connection to you more than anything. So the sixth step of advanced marketing is getting really good at marketing in alignment for you and not doing things outside of alignment for you. Not stepping out of things that bring you joy, not stepping out of things that you feel powerful in, not stepping out of things you just genuinely wanna do.

So, for example, sometimes I have time and I’ll just quickly record videos on my Insta story and say what I’m thinking about in the moment. I don’t do it very often, but every once in a while, I just get on there and I start going. And the way that the algorithm works and typical buyers work right now in the world, typical engagers on social media, they want to read captions because they don’t want to take the effort to click on the video and listen, except I don’t want to do that.

Sometimes it takes so long, and then you hit the caption, and then it like spins for five minutes, and then it tells you it’s unavailable, and by then I’ve lost the desire to do it. So instead, I only do things that I really like to do, so my energy is really pure and clean and exciting with everything I do. And that has, that creates a lot of power in everything you d,o is because it’s very intentional and it’s based on the things that bring you joy and what you would be excited to listen to or to read or to watch or to consume.

And then the last piece is we’re going to talk about tomorrow is communicating in the language of PSPR, which is the most potent form of communication that you could possibly do for people that will reach those early majority, reach those late majority and get the 60% of people that you just have to work a lot harder to reach, but you can’t do any of these things when you’re saying your audience isn’t big enough and you don’t have a big enough audience, when you believe your list is dead or it’s not good, or if you say things like if they wanted to buy, they already would have, or no one’s paying attention, they’re not interested, I don’t have demand, the market doesn’t take me seriously, I’m just a small business, anything like this, or if you’re fiddling with your offer, instead of solving for the above things. Or if you’re creating too big of strategies, trying to get more eyeballs because you’re not, all you want to do is get those innovators because they give you a hit, but they don’t make you develop the skillsets required to tap into the early and late majority where like the winfalls of money come from.

Okay, so that is advanced marketing and what we would really dive into for those of you who are considering 200k Mastermind, we’re gonna be talking about it a little bit every day, but these are the things that I have my students focusing on. These are the things that give you the most power in your business and have more of an impact than any of the things you might be currently spending your time on.

Hey, if you’re ready to make money as a life coach, I want to invite you to join my 2K for 2K program; where you’re going to make your first $2,000 the hardest part using my simple five-step formula for getting consults and closing new clients. Just head over to StaceyBoehman.com/2Kfor2K. We’ll see you inside.

title: Ep #336: Using Emotional Regulation to Build a 200k Business with Stéphanie Vautrin
transcript:
Welcome 
to the 
Make Money as a Life Coach
®
 
podcast
 
where sales expert and Master Coach Stacey Boehman teaches you how to make your first $2k, $20k, and $200k using her proven formula.

Hey coaches, today I have a really exciting episode planned for you. I have one of my past 200k, current 2 Million Dollar Group students here with me today to talk about making $200k and how she’s done it, and all about her business, and everything that she’s learned that she can share with you.

So, without further ado, please welcome Stéphanie Vautrin from France. I have to say it because we had a whole conversation about how I was going to have a hard time saying her name. But I think I did okay. Please introduce yourself. Tell everyone where you’re from, what you do in your coaching business, what your niche is, and anything else that you think would be relevant to the conversation.

Stéphanie Vautrin: Hello Stacey, hello everybody. I’m so happy to be here. It’s like when you rehearse for the Academy Award or something, like forever. And I’m like, that’s today, I’m on, that’s my time. I’ve been rehearsing in my bathroom for so long for this moment. It’s crazy.

Stacey: I love it.

Stéphanie: You know, I joined 2k in 2019.

Stacey: Wow.

Stéphanie: So it was like we were 500 when I joined, so it was very much the beginning of it.

Stacey: And I did not know that.

Stéphanie: Yeah. And I saw past rounds and rounds of 200k passing by. And at first, I was like, making a million? It doesn’t make any sense for me. And then the more the round came by, I was like, maybe someday. And it kind of grew on me until I reached the point where, okay, that’s my turn, actually. This is my time. I can reach $200k. And now I’m in 2 Million. I mean, are you kidding me? It’s like I’m just not… it’s like I’m still figuring this out. It’s crazy. It’s just crazy.

Stacey: That’s so amazing.

Stéphanie: I’m a childhood trauma coach. I work with people who went through, actually, quite regular childhoods from Boomer parents.

Stacey: Yeah.

Stéphanie: Meaning no room for emotions, a lot of neglect, emotional neglect, and because they were not aware of what they were doing emotionally, basically, we had a roof over our heads. Sorry for the accent, maybe it’s a bit confusing at some point.

Stacey: No, I’m following. I’m here with you.

Stéphanie: If you have a roof above your head, food on the table, and you have clothes on, there’s nothing to complain about. Yeah. So that created a lot of trauma, actual trauma, in a lot of people. So I’m here for those people. I’m here to free them from the impact this had on their life, the survival mode this has created on their life. So when you work with me, basically, in a couple of months, you get rid of procrastination because of the survival mode, or freeze mode. You get rid of chronic stress or anxiety, one of those.

Stacey: Wow. I was getting ready to ask how does this tend to show up for people when they have childhood trauma. So it’s procrastination, freeze mode, not getting done, chronic stress. Anything else that you see a lot of?

Stéphanie: Burnout is like a symptom, a result of a survival mode, but that’s a fight mode. That’s not the freeze mode; it’s a fight mode. It’s the nervous system state where you just need to be in action because otherwise, you feel the stress inside of you, but then you have this limited energy. And when you don’t listen to your body, at some point, you just burn out of energy, and your body says, “Okay, this strategy doesn’t work. So, you know what we’re going to do? We’re going to switch to freeze mode.” That’s like a saving mode, energy-wise. You save your energy because giving too much energy away doesn’t work anymore, so we’re going to go for this one.

Stacey: Yeah, that’s so interesting. I always talk about burnout as people tend to solve it with all-or-nothing thinking, so they go from one end to the other. And I’ve never heard it said this way, but it’s 100% true. The ends of the all-or-nothing thinking spectrum or black and white thinking around burnout is freeze mode or fight mode. Right? I’m either going to fight really hard and burn out, or I’m just going to not do anything and be a little bit frozen instead of that middle ground.

I think this is very interesting. So do you find that the link from childhood trauma, from being in if you were raised kind of without emotional intelligence and without an ability to process emotions and understand what those are, then there’s a lot of shoving down emotions that happens.

And I’m reading Dr. Becky’s 
Good Inside
, very slowly, because I have a toddler. But I am going to finish it. And one of the things that she was talking about is when one of the greatest things that we can do as parents is model emotional processing and emotional regulation, and emotional intelligence. If we can do anything with our children, the best thing we can do is just model what we do with our emotions when they come up and how to handle them, and how to be with them. And she talks about how a lot of people are taught that if they have an explosive emotion, I’m bad, and I’m wrong, and I’m unacceptable, and I’m not liked, so shove it down. If I have any shame, shove it down, shove it all down.

So I can see how, as an adult, my guess is, then if you’ve just learned your whole life, if I have an emotion, shove it down, then you get very far away from the relationship with your body where you know what it’s saying to you. And if you don’t know what your body’s saying to you, then you don’t know how to stop before you burn out. You don’t know how to get started when you’re in freeze mode. There are things that are happening in your mind and your body, and you’re trying to operate in the world without the tools to really work with the things you want to do. And so you’re just constantly working against it. And I can imagine that’s what creates the chronic stress. Am I on the right track?

Stéphanie: For sure, for sure. And the thing is that we’ve learned when we’re a child to overuse our brain to solve things because the world when we were a child didn’t make any sense. Why am I here if I don’t feel connected to my parents? If I don’t feel love, if I have to chase the love, the validation, the connection, the security, it doesn’t make any sense. And usually, this kind of conscientiousness…?

Stacey: Contentiousness? That would be a hard one in another language. I love it.

Stéphanie: …happens around seven years old because this is the age of reason. This is the age where your brain connects the emotional part of the brain to reason, the capacity to resonate, to, no, resonate, to make reason. That’s correct.

Stacey: Maybe. I’m the worst at vocabulary. I think you’re asking, is it reasoning? Like it connects reasoning? Yeah.

Stéphanie: And usually, because I talk to inner children in my work, when this kind of realization of “Why the hell am I here?” happens, it’s when you’re seven because this connection happened. And the child just looks at his world, and it doesn’t make any sense. So because it didn’t make any sense, you have to use your brain a lot to try to make sense, to connect the, okay, so if they don’t like me, it’s because I’m not lovable, I’m not likable. It’s my fault. It’s all on me because it cannot be on my parents.

Because if it’s on them, then I’m screwed because I still have 11 years to go, minimum, and I’m stuck with them. So it has to be me; it cannot be them. I cannot see them any other way than it’s all my fault. And also, because the parents, because they were not responsible emotionally, they blame the children for their own emotions.

Stacey: Yeah. Oh yes.

Stéphanie: So you see how you grow up, and you’re charged with all that background, your backpack, on you emotionally. And then you arrive when you’re a grown-up, and you kind of don’t want to take responsibility for all those emotions because it’s too painful. So that’s why you scroll on TikTok, that’s why you eat the cookie, that’s why you binge, whatever. Because you have to run away from those emotions because they are unbearable; they are too painful.

Stacey: Yeah. Or just why you blame the world, right? It’s because it’s so painful to go inward, so it has to be outside things that are causing it, instead of there’s this internal turmoil. That’s so interesting. I recently saw, I’ve seen this actually a lot. It’s come up on my, I get a lot of kids stuff on my Instagram, but it’s really heartbreaking to think about. It said that if you yell at your kids and you say mean things to them like they’re stupid or why’d you do that and just things that are shaming them a little bit or you’re yelling at them or you’re, any type of just behavior that isn’t your love and connection and kindness, that it doesn’t teach them to not like you and not love you. It teaches them to not love themselves.

That hit me like every time, the first, I’ll cry now thinking about it. When I heard that, I was like, oh my gosh. That is so true. They will internalize it as I am wrong, I am bad. It has to be me. It’s definitely not them, especially because your parents are authority figures as well. So, what powerful work that you are doing for people in the world.

Stéphanie: Yeah, I totally agree with you and that’s actually my own parenthood that draw me to this work because I always swore to myself that I will never be my parents. I would never end up being like my parents. And when my older son turned not even one, I started slapping him on his hands because he was throwing food on the floor. And at the time, I was like, yeah, but what other solution do I have? That’s what I’ve been taught. I did not…

Stacey: Yeah.

Stéphanie: …think like that at the time. It was like, I’m powerless with this behavior, so the only thing I can do is this. This is the only way I know how to cope with this situation. But then I was like, slapping cannot be the only solution. That’s how I turned into nonviolent parenting, and I started listening to shows, reading books, getting trained.

Later on, I discovered the nervous system, and it all made sense. And that’s actually when I had to, because I moved abroad and then we came back, and I had to go live with my mother for one month in 2022. And living with her and my kids, I was like back in childhood, like back to how I felt powerless and unheard, misunderstood, no communication, angry, frustrated. I was back to when I was seven. And I saw how I was behaving with my kids, and I saw how my kids were behaving because of how I was feeling. And it was like, oh my god, this all makes sense. It’s like I had this epiphany of everything makes sense.

And you have to know that at this point in my business, I was struggling. I was making between $10k to $20k a year between 2017 and 2022, when I started my coaching business. And at this time, I had worked on myself. Started working with the rejection wound, which was my big one, and why I was in freeze mode and not being capable of marketing my business regularly.

At the same time, I started making videos on TikTok. And I had this raw material in front of me, like everything makes sense. I have to share it with the world. I mean, it’s very painful at the same time, but at the same time, it’s like, I think I discovered the cure for cancer, seriously. I think I’m really onto something, and finally, my business is aligned because I know what I want to talk about forever.

Stacey: Yeah, that’s amazing. So were you, what were you coaching on before you found this, before you had this epiphany when you were making the $10,000 to $20,000 a year for those five years? Were you just general coaching? Were you coaching on a little bit of everything? What kind of, do you even remember?

Stéphanie: Yeah, that’s what I was about to say. It was very vague. At some point, it was human design because I got some answers with human design, and then it was pivot, business, like when you change careers. Mindset coaching. It was very vague. I couldn’t really grasp it. And this is also what I want to talk about on your podcast is that if you’re at this stage of your business, don’t give up. I know it’s so hard. I mean, my husband was so tired of seeing me struggle with my business, and he had lost all hope that it would work someday.

But it all makes sense now. When I had this epiphany of, “Oh, I understand why it was so hard and why I had to go through all this,” it makes so much sense now that it’s all aligned. And seriously, I have to tell you the whole story. So, 2022 was the worst year ever. I made $2500 for the whole year at the end of August 2022. So, no money. I signed nobody. I got only nos. I had $2500 from recurring clients.

So, in July, I was at my mom’s for one month. My world was upside down. And at the same time, I was creating three TikToks a day because I made an engagement with myself that I would post every day for six months on TikTok, and then I would find a job. August, I could see that some videos started taking off. I got some messages from people. I saw that there was some interest in the topic I was bringing. September, like the real beginning of September, I signed my first client, and then I was like, that’s it, boom. Let’s go, baby, we’re on it. Let’s go. And I ended the year at $31k.

Stacey: Wow. That’s insane. So you were at $2500 in August, and by the end of the year you were at $31,000.

Stéphanie: Yeah. In December, I was making $10k months, and I was like, that was insane. I mean, $31k, I’d never made $31k. It didn’t make any sense. But when your body is regulated, when you’re in security in your life—because after my mom, I found a place of my own with my husband and my kids, and everything was back to normal—I found my routine, I felt secure, my kids were secure, and I could just focus on my business as much as I wanted.

So that’s how I started signing clients and everything. And since then, I’ve just kept growing and growing, and I’m unstoppable.

Stacey: That’s insane. Do you mind if you share a couple more numbers? What did you do after the $31,000 year? What was 2023 like? I’m curious about your growth trajectory after that because I know so many, hundreds of coaches who have been stuck at $10,000 or $20,000 or $30,000 for four or five years. And I have these conversations with them where their spouses are questioning the business, and they are questioning the business, and they’re tired and they’re wondering if they can sustain any longer, and they’re wondering what’s the point.

And I’m always telling them there are so many stories of people that I have known. I had a client who went 10 years without ever making money in her business, and then within two years she had made her first million dollars. Actually, I think she made her first $2 million. It was so fast. Stacey: Yeah.

Stéphanie: That’s what you did, and that’s what I did as well. I was the strong will, I was the problematic child, I was the one who was not supposed to succeed because she was not following the path of the family; she was disturbing the family structure, and so on. And I was not supposed to be successful. And I mean, it’s our role. And my son is the same; he’s the family…

Stacey: The family disruptor. I really love that term. Like…

Stéphanie: Exactly. And he disrupted me because he showed me another path, another way. Usually, of… ingraining power over him. It’s like, “Okay, what if you try choice? Like, give me a choice. Wouldn’t it be better if I have a choice?” “Okay, so you want to brush your teeth, or I brush your teeth?” “You want to try brushing your teeth? Okay, brush your teeth.” “Oh, that works, actually. That’s okay, that’s interesting. Oh.” You know, so these little things that when you start implementing them, and it’s actually not a danger to you that your kid gets the power to decide for himself, because that’s the best tool you can give him.

Stacey: Oh, that’s so good.

Stéphanie: You’ll have the power to make good decisions yourself, and I trust you with the decisions you make. And if the decision you make is not 100% efficient, I’m here for you. No problems. No grudges against the fact that you made your own choice. No problem. I actually teach you how to make them. And that’s such a… that makes my kids… I have two kids. That would make their life so much easier than what I had to go through, stressing about all the decisions I made, like, “Did I make a good decision? Did I…?” And thinking about the past decision and the future decision. Oh my god.

This is so much energy wasted because we haven’t been taught how to take decisions for ourselves and trust that we are capable of taking good decisions because our parents, in the power struggle, were taking decisions for us. That’s the problem with authority education or authoritative education, is that you lose your power because the parent holds all the power, and the kid has none. So it’s just kind of, “Okay, I cannot trust myself because I don’t have power anyway. I’m not capable anyway, so…”

Stacey: It’s so good. That’s so good. Okay, so we are at time. This conversation flew by. And one of the things I love is that in every conversation I have when I bring people on, something different comes up. What did it take to get to $200k? What helped you rapidly grow? And in this conversation, the thing I’ve taken is that in so many different scenarios, it’s been emotional regulation. And I don’t think I’ve ever gotten to have this type of conversation before on the podcast. We’ve talked about different things with different people, but not this specific conversation. I think it’s going to be so valuable for so many people.

But I love to ask this question because I know you said you prepared a lot for the podcast, and it shows. Is there anything else that we haven’t talked about that you wanted to share with the audience, that you wanted them to hear about your journey, about making $200k, about anything that we just haven’t covered yet?

Stéphanie: Well, actually, we have covered it, but I think it’s important to emphasize it.

Stacey: Okay.

Stéphanie: Is that the belief you had to grow up with, the emotion that feels very heavy, like shame. Shame is a very big one. It really breaks us into pieces, and it makes us hide, and binge, and treat ourselves very badly because we were shamed when we were kids. And this is not your shame. This is not your heaviness, the weight that you’re carrying; it’s not yours. It’s something that your parents put on your shoulders when you were a child.

So when you feel that heaviness, what I do with my clients is I make my clients give back their emotional burden to their parents. And it’s never like… sometimes they would tell me, “No, but I don’t want to hurt them. I don’t want to make them feel this or that.” And I’m telling them, I’m not telling you to call them and tell them that they were awful parents. That’s not what I’m saying. It’s an energetical work that we’re doing. You just symbolically give back what they gave you that… they were confused, they didn’t know. This did not belong to you; it belongs to them. So give it back to them.

So, to all the people who are listening, when you feel like you’re stuck in this inner struggle of shame, of you’re spinning and you think you’re the worst person and you’re never going to make it, and you feel so heavy in yourself, just think about, “Okay, I’m carrying burdens that are not mine, and I’m symbolically going to give it back to my parents and free myself from it because it’s not mine. I have nothing to be shameful about. I don’t have to keep believing that I am shameful. This doesn’t bring anything to my life, and above all, not to my business, and even more, not to your clients.”

Because your clients don’t need a coach who is ashamed of himself, because your clients probably are ashamed of themselves. So it’s not helping, and it’s for sure not selling. So give back those emotions to your parents because this is going to make your life so much easier, for real, so much easier.

Stacey: So good. I remember Byron Katie, I think it was Byron Katie, who said, “Your parents did the best they could with the knowledge they had at the time,” or something similar. And that’s been really helpful for me to think about. It’s like, that was… the way you talked about it at the beginning is if you have Boomer parents, that’s the way they were raised, too. They don’t… my mom’s childhood mirrors exactly the childhood that we had with her. It was the exact same. And we just get the opportunity to break that generational pattern and do something different.

And I do think as a society, just in general, our generation is very much wanting to do that and to learn more and to understand the “littles” a lot, and their psychology and what helps them grow, and understand ourselves on the same path.

But that’s really helpful for me. It’s like, it doesn’t have to be a power struggle of blame of someone else. It’s just they did the best they could with what they knew and how they were raised, and now we just get to decide, do we want to keep doing that? Do we want to keep creating that pattern? And I love to think that all coaches, we’re all… what do we call it? The rule breakers. We’re all the change-makers. We are all the family… what did you call it?

Stéphanie: Black sheep, disruptor, or black sheep also.

Stacey: The family disruptors. I was definitely the black sheep. That’s what I would call it, but I love “family disruptor.” That’s so good. Because sometimes things need to be disrupted, so it’s okay. That is us. That is entrepreneurship, that is coaching. We are the disruptors. So fun.

Stéphanie: Yeah.

Stacey: Thank you so much for being here.

Stéphanie: You’re welcome. My pleasure, really my pleasure. I’m happy I rehearsed so much because…

Stacey: It was such a powerful conversation. If people want to see your awesome videos, I’m going to… so you sent me one about getting into 200k, and it was you and your mom—you playing your mom and you—and that one was so great. I have saved it because I’m going to play it on my social media the week before this comes out, just to tease it and get people really excited about it.

So I’ve been saving it, but I watched it, and I was like, “Oh my god, this is everything.” Maybe it was your acceptance video; I don’t remember. Something was sent to me, and I was like, “This is everything. We have to have this and use it when we have her on the podcast.” And then I got pregnant and I was so sick, so we had to move this back a while, but it’s perfect. I’m going to release that.

But if people want to see all of your videos and they want to follow you and they want to learn from you, where are all the platforms you’re on? I know you’re on TikTok. Can you give us… we’ll put all of this in the show notes, but can you say it for them as well?

Stéphanie: So it’s Steph La Coach. Like “La Coach” is in French. Steph La Coach.

Stacey: So S T E P H L A coach. Oh my god. I’m literally looking at your name on Zoom, so I don’t know what just happened in my brain. S T E P H L A coach. Okay.

Stéphanie: So it’s on TikTok, it’s Steph La Coach. It’s on Instagram, Steph La Coach, and on Facebook, it’s Stéphanie Vautrin. So it’s my… Vautrin, in French. It’s my family name.

Stacey: I love it. So fun. We will also put this in the show notes, and we’ll tag you as well when we post the podcast and your video and everything on social, so people will be able to find you. But it’s definitely worth a watch on your videos because I also think sometimes we get stuck in, “I have to build my business this way because this is the way I’ve been seeing other people do it. And so this is the way Stacey does it, this is the way Brooke does it, this is the way someone else does it.” And I really love that you found a very genuine, authentic way to market your business that you love and you’re so good at.

I would never be able to do these, but I actually did do improv, and I did love it. But they’re just so unique to you, and I think it’s such an example of what’s possible when you decide… I always tell people, you don’t have to do the thing I do. You have to do the thing that you would love to do. I started live streaming the day Facebook Live made live streaming available. I don’t even remember what year it was, but the day I saw a live stream, I was like… and they were like, “Oh yeah, this came on the platform today.” And I was like, “I’m going live.”

But that was my thing, and I loved it, and I was so good at it. And so I think that people try to fit themselves into, “I have to do it this way. I have to have the email list, or I have to run ads, or I have to post on social every day.” But it’s really what lights you up, and you’re a really great example of that. So I think people should definitely look you up and see how you’re doing your thing. It’s so good.

Stéphanie: Thank you so much. So this is because when you were a kid, again, you were told that being you was not secure, was not okay. You could not be yourself. You could not explore who you were because the frame of exploration that your parents gave you was so little, and they were answering their needs and not your needs. So you learned that being you was unsafe.

So you grow up, and you have to compare yourself. You have to look outside of yourself for the answers of, “Who am I? What am I supposed to do? Where am I supposed to go?” When you have all the answers inside of you, but you have to trust that you have them inside of you and that what you do is only you can do it. And so you have to listen to those voices who tell you, yeah, just put your jacket, like your little granny, I don’t know how you call it, put your little pullover on… and just play your mom and have fun with it… 

Stacey: Like a shawl, like your granny shawl.

Stéphanie: Shawl, yes, exactly, your shawl. Put on your shawl and just think about how your mom was reacting when you were… the last time you had her on the phone. I was like, “Yeah, okay, let’s do that.” You know, just have fun, for real. Just have fun with what’s fun for you. That is fun for me, but maybe it’s not fun for you. So find what is your fun or what’s igniting you from the inside when you think about it.

Stacey: That’s so good. What a beautiful note to end on. Find what ignites you, what excites you, what is your fun. People forget, you have to have fun marketing. If you don’t have fun marketing, people feel that. They feel the energy of “have to” versus “I want to, I get to.” This is going to be fun. So good. Thank you so much for coming on.

Stéphanie: Thank you for having me.

Stacey: Yeah. So fun. I’m so happy to have you. Your story is so inspiring. What a great podcast. Alright, so everyone knows how to follow Stéphanie. Thank you all for listening, and we will talk to you next week.

Hey, if you’re ready to make money as a life coach, I want to invite you to join my 2k for 2k program; where you’re going to make your first $2,000 the hardest part using my simple five-step formula for getting consults and closing new clients. Just head over to StaceyBoehman.com/2kfor2k. We’ll see you inside.

title: Ep #335: 3 Types of 200k Businesses & Scaling Time
transcript:
Welcome 
to the 
Make Money as a Life Coach
®
 
podcast
 
where sales expert and Master Coach Stacey Boehman teaches you how to make your first $2K, $20K, and $200K using her proven formula.

Hey coaches, welcome to episode 335. So today is the third episode of our three-part series, launching in one week based on the three most popular revenue groups that we come in. It’s not all of the revenue groups. We have students who come in at $50k and $60k and $150k and all the revenues, but typically I boil it down to my $25k earners, my $100k earners, my $200k earners. And then of course, people fall in between.

So today we’re going to be talking about my $200k earners, people making $200k for the first time, people at $200k, and what the data study revealed about this income group that I feel like I’ve been preaching to the choir for many years, but the numbers really, I think, show it. And so I want to break it down and talk you through it. And so we’re going to talk about three types of $200k businesses and the different levels of value that each one of them have.

And how you might want to transition your $200k business. So, the first things first, when one of the things that the numbers showed us is that we have created or had 86 brand new $200k earners created in the $200k room. Like from scratch, 86 people made $200k for the first time, and then 28 made more than a $200k return coming into the room.

So that’s 114 students in a five-year period creating $200k or more. So some of them might have created $300k, some of them might have created $400k. And then their median growth was 14% in one round and 28% annualized.

Now, this was not shocking to me at all. And I’m here on this episode to educate you and prepare you on why. But first, it’s important to know that growth is the people making $200k is not the people making $200k for the first time, it’s the group coming in already at $200k. So between $200k and $300k.

This is a part where I’ve been teaching this for quite a while. This is a time in your business where things start to slow down. For good reasons, and only in the perspective of revenue, there’s a lot happening underneath the surface, but this is a time where once your growth starts getting in the multiple six figures, strategy matters, being strategic, having your back end cleaned up, and really preparing to scale is where you want to be focused.

I’m going to break this down for you because if you don’t understand the three types of $200k businesses and why growth could start slowing down around this revenue period between $200k and $300k, it could cost you a lot of confidence. It could create a lot of heartache. It could keep you out of being in the current, out of the miracle, and out of growing fast.

And this is median growth. So it doesn’t mean this is everyone’s growth. There are also people who come in and they explode at $200k, and they go from $200k to $400k. You know, for me, I went from $325,000 to $860,000 in a calendar year. But I leveraged everything I’m going to tell you on this episode. And I stayed in the miracle of it all.

But what I think is really like amazing about these numbers is I think there’s so much, you know, information marketing in the industry that’s very focused on, you know, quantum leaps and it’s like constantly like double and triple your revenue, like all of the time, year after year. And what I’ve found is a lot of people end up coming to me very exhausted and with a perspective on their business that doesn’t quite align with real-world businesses.

And remember, 40% annualized growth is hypergrowth. Right? For even like venture startups that have millions of dollars of venture capital running through them, like tech startups, like that 40% is considered hypergrowth. So 28% is still a lot of growth. But we’re getting a lot of messages in the industry that’s like, you know, you should be doubling your revenue, 100% growth, 200% growth. And yes, I’ve had a podcast where I said, like my the median growth of my $25k earners is 248%. That’s just the fact.

And also, they have room to grow. When you get to a business that’s $200,000 and $300,000, you don’t always have that room to grow. Sometimes you do. There are so many factors that go into it. But we’re going to break it down today, and I’m going to give you a real-world perspective so that you maybe don’t have to feel so alone or like you’ve done it wrong or something has gone terrible.

Like sometimes just what we make our numbers mean causes us to completely spin out, step out of our self-concept, lose our minds, hate our businesses, think we’re failing, and destroy everything we’ve created, but only because we made our numbers mean that something has gone wrong. And then you like have an outside perspective of outside of the industry of maybe what people have been marketing to you and you’re like, oh wait, actually, tech companies in Silicon Valley are growing 40% annually and that’s considered hypergrowth. Maybe I’m doing great if I’m growing 30% every year.

So I want to bring this conversation as we make more and more money back to a little bit more of like reality without also telling you what’s not possible because I went from $325,000 to $860,000. But I will say I was highly mentored during that time. I had a lot of the things we’re going to talk about on this episode. I had a lot of the skills developed already. I developed them between $150,000 and $325,000. I also didn’t have kids at the time. I worked like my business was my baby. It got 100% of my focus during this time, every ounce of me. And I really just, like there were so many things working.

There was also things that were not working, but there were so many things that were working during this time period where 100%, like these types of quantum leaps absolutely can happen. And if they’re not, it’s also okay. Like nothing has gone wrong. Okay.

So let’s break it down. Let’s talk about the three types of $200k businesses. The first type of $200k business is a 200… And this is not inclusive of everything. There are also $200k businesses that are memberships and courses, and things like that. I’m going to be speaking to typically the businesses that I coach on and what I see, but I do have outliers come in. I have people who come in who have memberships and things like that. Memberships, courses, programs. But typically, at the $200k level, what I see coming in is $200k in one-on-one coaching.

So you have maybe 20 clients a week, maybe you’re charging, you know, $10k for that coaching package or $5k for that coaching package, depending on, you know, what your package length is. But the first type of business is having a one-on-one coaching business making $200k.

And then the second one is a hybrid $200k business of one-on-one coaching and group coaching. And typically that’s small group coaching. But again, it could also be like a membership or a program.

And then the third type is a $200k business in group only. So you make $200,000, and maybe you have one or two groups that you run either annually or at the same time. You’re making money purely off of group coaching.

So here’s the first thing you need to know. These are not the same businesses. There are pros and cons to all of them and specific work for each business to create the business and to drive the business forward. And when I say specific work, I mean like skills you have to develop, self-coaching, you know, personal development work, business development work for each business to create the first $200k and then drive the business forward.

So let’s break them down. So $200k in a one-on-one coaching business is the simplest of the businesses. And that is really the pro of that. I remember having a $150,000 and a $325,000 business that was mostly one-on-one. I had started to also, at $325,000, I also already had groups as well. But this was a time in my life where it felt the easiest to sell, the easiest to deliver, the least amount of responsibility as far as like business demands. I was just immersed in coaching all of the time.

So I wasn’t spending a ton of time marketing, the things I and selling, like the things I was doing, were kind of selling themselves. I didn’t have to have a huge audience to do this, so it wasn’t, I just wasn’t having to think really big. I was mostly working off of referrals and networking.

And I just got to spend an immense amount of time in my craft with very little responsibilities. I didn’t have a VA because I didn’t need one. And it was really a beautiful time in my career. And I always tell people, the longer you can stay in this beautiful time of your career without holding yourself back, but like there doesn’t need to be a rush. Like this is a I can’t say it enough, a beautiful time in your business. And you can actually take a one-on-one coaching business to $300k or $400k. Like really as far as you want to go, the business work for this type of business is to grow your identity and therefore your demand so that you can keep raising your prices and keep filling ideal clients at that price point and keep delivering results at that price point so that you could, if you wanted to have a really simple business, grow it up to $300k, $400k.

So you have to find buyers at the new price point, and then you’ve got to overdeliver for what you’re charging. And that’s my value. You don’t have to do that. It’s just my value is I always want to overdeliver for everything I charge for.

So there’s not a lot of like work that you have to be doing. There’s not a lot of like skills you have to develop, tools you have to develop. It’s identity work. It’s believing in demand work. It’s finding buyers at your price point that you want to be at. It’s over delivering to the clients that you have, and then enjoying the crap out of your business. Super fun.

And then the next business is a $200k hybrid business of one-on-one and group. And for this business, the work is really being clear with the purpose and the value of each of these offers that you’re selling. If you’re selling one-on-one and group, you got to be clear and know the purpose of the value of each one of them without them being in competition with each other. So one-on-one cannot be in competition with group.

You can’t be selling them against each other. Group can’t be I tell this to my students all the time, group cannot be the cheaper version of your one-on-one. If you sell it that way, it’s not going to sell. It can’t be the discount. It can’t be for the people who can’t afford the one-on-one. The group has to be standalone value and purpose on its own. And then you have to create audiences to support both of those offers. You want to be constantly having your one-on-one spots filled, and you want to constantly be filling up your groups. And those aren’t always the same people.

So to give you an idea, when I did this business model, my one-on-one clients were also buying my group. Not for a discount, not for free, but because my self-concept and the value of my offer were aligned.

So, and I wasn’t pitting them against each other. It was just like, I have this one-on-one offer, and here’s what we do here with one-on-one, and here’s the value, here’s the purpose. Here’s this group. Here’s what we do in group, and here’s the value, and here’s the purpose here. And they’re both so amazing and they’re both so great and, you know, different people are going to buy each one, and also the same person might want to buy both.

And that’s great too. They both are worth it. They both have lots of value. That’s the work when you have a hybrid business. The work is also to create demand for both without dropping one and forgetting about one.

And this is I think the thing I coach on the most when people have a hybrid business is how am, I how do I market both? How do I make content for both of them? How does it all fit into place when you’re doing it for the first time?

And the work really is to not be confused about how to do this, but to get clarity quickly and then move forward powerfully in bringing these two offers to life. Like you want to just understand how you’re selling them, the purpose, the value, if you’re in my Mastermind, you want to be able to know what your PSPR is for each of them, who your client is for each of them. And then have that self-concept of I have two offers that are both in demand, and I sell them in that way.

I will tell you one thought I’ve given my Mastermind students that has been really helpful for them has been that I believe every time I show up to sell any of the offers that I have, I am selling for my entire brand. I’m selling all of my offers at the same time. So if I’m selling the Entrepreneur Series, I’m also selling 2k and 200k and 2 Million Dollar Group.

I get people asking me about each of them every time I do an Entrepreneur Series. And then when I sell 2k, the Entrepreneur Series always comes up. Someone’s always asking me about, well, when can I get into 200k? When I sell 200k, people are always asking me about 2 Million Dollar Group, and people will typically buy 2k while I’m selling 200k because it’s so inspiring to them. So I just believe that every time I show up, I’m selling for my entire brand. I’m selling all of my offers. I’m constantly showing the success of my offers and growing demand for all of them as I sell each of them.

So for you, if you have this hybrid business or you want to, you’ve got to know that you want to be growing demand for both as you sell one or the other. You’ll always have one-on-one people that will come in when you launch group. And then you’ll always have people that do consults for one-on-one, and you think they’re a better fit for group. And not because they don’t have the money to afford one-on-one. There’s a lot of other reasons someone could be a better fit for group.

But being super clear on this, that’s really the work of having two offers that are happening at the same time is they can’t compete with each other and you have to be really clear and you have to have audiences for both, demand for both and really understand your marketing plan for both.

And then the third offer is the $200k in making $200,000 a year all in group. And this offer, I’ve said that they’re not they don’t all have the same value, these businesses. And what I mean by that is a business who is making $200,000 all in group, or even if it’s $150,000 all in group. That business is going to be the most valuable business. Like if you thought of businesses being sold. Now, these are still businesses that are too small probably to be sold. But if you thought about like a business’s value meaning like what could it be sold for, what someone could buy into, the value of a business that is all in group making $200,000, it’s the highest value of the three. It’s also the hardest.

It’s the most valuable because it has the most time that is leveraged. If you think about it, if you have 20 clients and you’re you’re making $200k and you have 20 clients, then you are on the phone 20 hours a week delivering. So the one-on-one energy of you required to deliver that offer is very great.

But if you have one group and you’re making $200,000 from that one group, and maybe you launch it once or twice or three times a year, and it’s an hour or 90 minutes a week that you spend coaching in that group, that’s a very different thing. You know, it takes me 20 hours to deliver this offer and make this money, versus it takes me one hour to deliver this offer and make this money. So one entrepreneur has a lot more time. One entrepreneur has the ability to grow a lot more. And one probably has a much bigger audience because if you’re selling group and you’re making all $200,000 in that group, likely your audience is much bigger. So all of those things equal, you know, cha-ching, way more value. It’s more scalable.

But again, it’s also the hardest business to build. I am often baffled when entrepreneurs make the shift from $200k in one-on-one coaching, and again, 20 something hours on the phone, to $200k in one to two hours on calls, again, making the exact same money, but 18 less hours, 19 less hours on delivery. And they will think there’s no growth.

And this is what I mean by like the revenue might show that there’s no growth, or like say you went from $200k in one-on-one and then you made $230,000 in group. The revenue is going to show a smaller percent of growth. And if you just looked at that, you would think, oh, well, that’s not successful.

And this leaves me so stumped. Like I always imagine like eyes blinking, crickets chirping. Like the if you’ve seen the meme of the little blonde girl and she’s got buck teeth and she’s like looking at you side eye. It’s like a hugely famous meme. It’s how I feel inside when I hear people make this jump from one-on-one to group and they maintain $200k in revenue and they’re like, I haven’t had any growth.

And I’m like, what? First, in results alone, you gave yourself 18, 19 hours of your life back and leverage to build something else even bigger and make even more money. You just opened up the ability to maybe make $400k or $600k, or you opened up the ability to live.

Like you scaled your time. Right? There’s two things you can actually grow and scale. You can scale your money, but you can also scale your time. And time, you can’t get more of. You can create endless amounts of money, but you cannot create endless amounts of time. You have an exact amount.

And you will see the richest people in the world will tell you that time is the most valuable resource, not money. You don’t get the time back. So the more you can scale and give yourself time, then the more you open up yourself to be able to create more money. So you need the time first. It’s what I tell people when they want to have major growth jumps in revenue, no matter what it is. I talked about this on the 100k episode. If you get to $100k and you want to go from $100k to $200k or $100k to $300k, what’s required is energy. What’s required is, I have the capacity mentally, emotionally, and physically. I have the time to then do more, add more, add a marketing strategy, add a revenue stream. Like I have time and energy to give to this to grow.

title: Ep #333: Explosive Growth at 25k in Revenue
transcript:

 to the
